Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan wrote to me at midnight, and said that we must talk; and I knew, the moment I read his words, what their meaning was.

The next day we met at a coffee room in the town, where he was already seated, looking down at some little screen in his hand, as everybody's conduct in such cases is; and he looked not a little out of spirits. He said that he was not ready for any thing serious; and then, with the air of one who felt the occasion to require it, he added that the fault was not in me, but in himself.

I could have cried, but I did not; I only nodded, and said that it was all very well. I then walked home in the rain, and ate a whole pint of ice, which was at least consistent with the occasion.

My companion in the house with me thought that I made too much of it; and perhaps I did; but it hurt me, for all that.

lessons: The chief difference is that the draft names its feelings and its speech in short, flat declarations, where Austen builds balanced periods, reports speech in the narrator's syntax, and lets judgement out through abstract nouns and understatement. Practise joining clauses with semicolons and "and", and letting each paragraph carry one larger movement rather than a series of single-sentence turns.

outline.gist: Ryan's midnight text and the narrator's immediate foreboding.
The coffee shop meeting; Ryan is nervous and says he is not ready for something serious; it is not the narrator, it is him.
The narrator keeps composure, walks home in the rain, and eats a pint of ice cream.
The roommate calls it overreacting; the narrator half-concedes but remains hurt.

plan.gist: The midnight text and the narrator's immediate certainty of what it means.
plan.why: Begin at the event that announces the subject, so the reader enters already expecting a rupture and reads what follows for how it is borne.

plan.gist: The coffee shop encounter: Ryan nervous, speaking the breakup in his own words.
plan.why: Let the cause arrive through the man's speech and manner rather than through the narrator's explanation; the reader judges him as the narrator quietly does.

plan.gist: The narrator's outward composure, then the private walk in the rain and the pint of ice cream.
plan.why: Show the character first in self-command and then in private relief; the contrast makes the hurt felt without self-pity, and keeps the reader's sympathy.

plan.gist: The roommate's verdict and the narrator's half-admission that it still hurt.
plan.why: Close with a cooler, almost ironic outside judgment so the narrator's final 'it still hurt' lands as a modest truth rather than a complaint; the story is given a settled point.

faults.quote: he looked not a little out of spirits
faults.why: The draft says Ryan looked nervous. 'Out of spirits' means low or dejected, so the feeling shifts from anxiety to gloom.

faults.quote: as everybody's conduct in such cases is
faults.why: Adds a sweeping claim about everyone's behaviour that the writer never made. The grammar is also muddled: 'conduct' is made to match 'looking down at some little screen'.

faults.quote: as everybody's conduct in such cases is
faults.why: The clause is clumsy and ungrammatical. It reads as forced irony and does not sound like Austen's smooth generalisations.

faults.quote: with the air of one who felt the occasion to require it
faults.why: Invents a characterisation of Ryan, a theatrical air in delivering the line. The draft only says what he said, and this tilts the reader's judgement of him beyond it.

faults.quote: said that it was all very well
faults.why: The draft has her say 'okay', a plain acceptance. 'All very well' carries a reservation or irony that changes the tone of her reply.

faults.quote: I could have cried, but I did not
faults.why: 'I wanted to cry' becomes 'could have cried', which is a different thing: capacity, not desire.

faults.quote: which was at least consistent with the occasion
faults.why: An added ironic verdict on her own indulgence. The meaning is also murky: what is consistent with what? It undercuts the hurt the draft is expressing.

faults.quote: My companion in the house with me
faults.why: A laboured circumlocution for 'roommate'. Austen would say 'my companion' or 'the friend who lived with me'. It reads as a riddle.

faults.quote: ate a whole pint of ice,
faults.why: 'A pint of ice' is odd and ambiguous, and the notes quote it as 'ice-cream'. The sentence also trails off on its tail clause.

faults.quote: a coffee room in the town
faults.why: In Austen a coffee-room belongs to an inn. 'In the town' is a flat gloss of 'downtown'. The diction is period dress rather than period habit.

faults.quote: and I knew, the moment I read his words, what their meaning was.
faults.why: The inverted ending is stiff. Austen's first-person narrators, and her narrator generally, are more fluent and ironic, so this sounds like pastiche.

faults.quote: Judgement in abstract nouns: “he looked not a little out of spirits”
faults.why: The quoted phrase contains no abstract-noun judgement, and it is cited again for litotes. The move label does not match the example.

faults.quote: cites Lady Susan, ch. 24, ¶ 3
faults.why: Lady Susan is an epistolary novella arranged in letters, not chapters. The precise chapter and paragraph citations throughout look unverifiable or invented.

faults.quote: “I then walked home in the rain, and ate a whole pint of ice-cream, which was at least consistent with the occasion.”
faults.why: The note quotes 'ice-cream' and 'ice-cream' differently from the rewrite's 'ice'. The notes also never flag the substantive additions ('as everybody's conduct', 'with the air of one who...').

faults.quote: Practise joining clauses with semicolons and "and"
faults.why: The lesson is two sentences and generic. It gives no concrete before/after from this text and no reason why the moves work, and it does not mention the irony it relied on.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the events and order and has some period flavour, but it shifts several feelings (nervous to 'out of spirits', 'okay' to 'all very well') and adds ironic commentary that is clumsy ('as everybody's conduct in such cases is'). The notes mislabel moves and cite suspect chapter/paragraph sources, and the lesson is thin.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
A new family took possession of the next house at the close of the week, and brought with them a large cart and two little children; and the father, it was soon agreed, was very pleasant. The woman with him was of a reserved cast of countenance, which must be met with all one's own civility, and would pay back none of it.

My mother baked them biscuits at once, and carried them over herself, that she might learn where they came from, what the father did for a living, and whether they went to church; for she was not of a temper to be satisfied with a word over a wall.

It proved that the father was a lawyer, and single; or, to speak more exactly, parted from his wife. My mother received the account with a look which I understood at once; she had been labouring these many years to establish me, and here was a single man with a profession and two children, settled, as one might say, at her very door.

If the mom is the dad's wife or partner, the two statements contradict; if she is not, the reader is not told who she is. I made the standoffish woman simply "the woman with him," not his wife, so that his being single and parted from a former wife can stand, and the standoffish figure is kept without adding any new fact about her.

plan.gist: A new family moves in next door, with a truck and two kids.
plan.why: Begin with the arrival, the news that sets everything in motion; the reader sees the occasion before the scheme, exactly as Austen opens Pride and Prejudice with the newcomer's arrival.

plan.gist: The dad seems nice; the woman with him is standoffish.
plan.why: Establish the man as promising and the woman as not the point; the reader needs to see him clearly before learning he is free, so that the fact matters.

plan.gist: The narrator's mother bakes cookies and asks where they came from, what they do, whether they go to church.
plan.why: Show the mother's method through action rather than statement; the reader sees her as a busy matchmaker before the significant fact is known.

plan.gist: The dad is a lawyer and single, well, divorced.
plan.why: Place the crucial fact last among the particulars, so it lands as the hinge: like the mother, the reader has been gathering intelligence, and "single" changes everything.

plan.gist: The mother gets a look; the narrator knows exactly what she is thinking, having been the target for years.
plan.why: Close on the daughter's wry recognition, the comic point; it tells the reader what the whole little scene was for, and leaves the mother's design plain without needing to state it.

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother ("The mom is kind of standoffish"), but your second says the dad is single, well, divorced. If the mom is the dad's wife or partner, the two statements contradict; if she is not, the reader is not told who she is.
sense.resolution: Change "The mom is kind of standoffish" to "The woman with him is kind of standoffish." That removes the suggestion that she is the dad's wife, so the later "single, well, divorced" can stand, and it keeps the standoffish figure without adding any new fact about her.

sense.problem: The passage truly echoes the opening of Pride and Prejudice: a single newcomer of good fortune arrives in the neighbourhood, and a mother immediately schemes to marry her child to him.
sense.resolution: The rewrite may take from it the mother's eager fact-finding about the newcomer's circumstances, the swift turn from "single" to matchmaking intent, and the daughter's wry, knowing awareness of her mother's design.

faults.quote: a large cart
faults.why: The writer's 'huge truck' is replaced by a period object, which changes the thing described. The notes do not mention it.

faults.quote: and carried them over herself
faults.why: This adds an action the writer never gave. It is not reported as a liberty.

faults.quote: it was soon agreed, was very pleasant
faults.why: The writer gave one narrator's impression ('seems nice'). The rewrite invents a consensus ('agreed') with no one named, and 'very pleasant' is stronger than 'seems nice'.

faults.quote: a single man with a profession and two children, settled, as one might say, at her very door
faults.why: This adds the narrator's gloss and shifts the closing beat. The writer's final point was that the mother has tried to set her up 'for years'. The rewrite ends on the neighbour's proximity, which weakens that emphasis.

faults.quote: The woman with him was of a reserved cast of countenance
faults.why: The mending is weak. 'The woman with him' still reads as a partner, so the contradiction with 'single' is only blurred, not resolved. The children's mother is left unaccounted for. The woman is never plainly identified as a sister, housekeeper or other relation.

faults.quote: which must be met with all one's own civility, and would pay back none of it
faults.why: The grammar is garbled. A 'cast of countenance' is made the thing that 'would pay back' civility, and the sentence shifts between abstract and personal subjects. It reads as a riddle, and the harsher 'pay back none' overstates 'kind of standoffish'.

faults.quote: parted from his wife
faults.why: 'Well, divorced' is a rueful correction. 'Parted from his wife' is vaguer and loses the writer's quick self-correction.

faults.quote: A new family took possession of the next house at the close of the week
faults.why: The Austen cadence is imitated mainly through semicolons and 'and' chains. It lacks her characteristic ironic generalization and free indirect judgement, so it reads partly as period costume.

faults.quote: cites Emma, ch. 29, ¶ 40
faults.why: The chapter and paragraph citations look unverifiable or invented, and they are not clearly apt for the moves claimed. The same applies to the Mansfield Park citations.

faults.quote: Understatement and litotes: “a reserved cast of countenance, which must be met with all one's own civility, and would pay back none of it”
faults.why: The quoted line is not litotes. It also reuses the sentence already cited for 'judgement in abstract nouns', which pads the notes.

faults.quote: The passage truly echoes the opening of Pride and Prejudice ... The rewrite takes from that scene the mother's eager fact-finding
faults.why: This is labelled a sense note but mends nothing. It wrongly says the rewrite 'takes' material from Pride and Prejudice, when it only keeps the writer's own content. It also assumes the narrator is a daughter ('her mother'), which the draft does not state.

faults.quote: which points the joke without adding any fact
faults.why: The liberty notes claim nothing is added. The rewrite does add inferred content ('settled ... at her very door') and the action of carrying the biscuits over, and these are unreported.

faults.quote: Practise holding several clauses in one sentence
faults.why: The lesson is a single, fairly generic syntax tip. The notes do not show concretely how to move from the writer's own short sentences to the Austen version, and the outline offers little beyond the writer's order.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the story and order, and Austenish periods and diction are present. But the standoffish-woman fix is only half-resolved, one key sentence is garbled, a few things are added or altered without comment, and the notes have dubious citations and a mislabelled sense note.

Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam
rewrite:
My dear friends,

The business will not take place on Tuesday as was proposed, but on Thursday; and the change is of such a nature as to require your early attention, for the persons who hold the matter in their keeping have not yet set their seal to the page of prices, and I should be sorry that it should go out into the world imperfect.

Let every part which belongs to you be finished by Wednesday at noon; and whoever finds himself detained, let him tell me of it today rather than tomorrow, for there will then be time enough to set things to rights, and none will be left behind. Delay, as is usual in these matters, would answer no purpose but its own.

With thanks, Sam

lessons: Your brief is telegraphic—clipped commands in two-word sentences—where Austen's manner builds a period that gathers the news and the reason for it into one balanced sentence, the point arriving last. Practise joining a fact with its consequence by "and" or a semicolon, and letting the narrator's mild formality (never her haste) carry the request.

plan.gist: Address the team.
plan.why: Name the audience first so everyone knows the message is theirs before any business is proposed.

plan.gist: Announce that the launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday.
plan.why: Put the changed date first because it alters all later work; no reader should go on acting on Tuesday.

plan.gist: Give the cause: Legal has not signed off on the pricing page, and Sam will not ship without it.
plan.why: Attach the cause to the change immediately, so the team reads the new date as necessity rather than caprice.

plan.gist: Ask for deck sections by Wednesday at noon.
plan.why: Place the request after the reason, so the deadline follows as the natural consequence of the new launch date, and Wednesday noon is understood in relation to Thursday.

plan.gist: If blocked, tell Sam today, not tomorrow.
plan.why: Put the contingency last as the call to act now, after the deadline has been fixed, so it sharpens rather than distracts from the request.

plan.gist: Thanks and signature.
plan.why: Close courteously and fix the sender, leaving the team on a cooperative note.

faults.quote: for there will then be time enough to set things to rights, and none will be left behind
faults.why: Invents a reassurance and a consequence (time enough, no one left behind) that Sam never states. It goes beyond commentary on what is there.

faults.quote: Let every part which belongs to you be finished by Wednesday at noon
faults.why: The deck is dropped. 'Every part which belongs to you' no longer says these are sections of a deck, so a fact is lost.

faults.quote: The business will not take place on Tuesday
faults.why: 'The launch' becomes the vague 'the business', which loses the specific event. Likewise 'the persons who hold the matter in their keeping' blurs Legal and the pricing sign-off.

faults.quote: the change is of such a nature as to require your early attention
faults.why: Adds a claim that the change demands attention, which is not in the draft. It also delays the reason and adds weight Sam did not give.

faults.quote: Delay, as is usual in these matters, would answer no purpose but its own.
faults.why: A riddling, near-meaningless aphorism. It reads as pastiche and does not clearly follow from the 'tell me today' request.

faults.quote: and none will be left behind
faults.why: Odd and unmotivated in a note about a deck deadline; it reads as strained period filler.

faults.quote: set their seal to the page of prices
faults.why: Over-periphrastic. Austen would not call the pricing page 'the page of prices', and the image is a costume rather than her idiom.

faults.quote: My dear friends,
faults.why: Too intimate and effusive for a team announcement. Austen's address to a body of people would be more measured.

faults.quote: Paragraph 2: ... Paragraph 3: ...
faults.why: The paragraph numbering is off: 'Paragraph 1' is the greeting and 'Paragraph 4' the sign-off, while the real body paragraphs are labelled 2 and 3. The notes appear misaligned with the text.

faults.quote: Understatement and litotes: “the persons who hold the matter in their keeping have not yet set their seal to the page of prices”
faults.why: This is periphrasis, not litotes or understatement. The label misdescribes the move.

faults.quote: Judgement in abstract nouns: “imperfect”
faults.why: 'Imperfect' is an adjective, not an abstract noun, so the label is wrong.

faults.quote: cites Lady Susan, ch. 40, ¶ 2
faults.why: Lady Susan is an epistolary novella with no chapter 40 in that form. Several other citations (Persuasion ch. 22 ¶14, Emma ch. 46 ¶17) look unverifiable and over-precise.

faults.quote: A framing the invitation invites: the consequence of promptness stated generally, a quiet reassurance
faults.why: Garbled phrasing. It also mislabels the sentence, which is about delay, not promptness. The reassurance it describes is invented content that the note passes off as a liberty.

faults.quote: clipped commands in two-word sentences
faults.why: Inaccurate about the writer's draft, which has no two-word sentences. The lesson is also thin and only partly matches the rewrite, where the reason, not the point, comes last.

judge.verdict: A plausible Austen pastiche that keeps the email's shape and most of its facts. It drops 'deck', blurs 'launch' and Legal, and invents a reassurance and a vague aphorism. The notes have misaligned paragraph numbers, mislabelled moves and doubtful citations, so the teaching value is weak.

Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
Our town might do well to close Main Street to carriages at the end of every week. The placing of a carriage in the town is a situation of no small distress, and the pavements are far too narrow for carriages of another kind. Places, indeed, there are which have done the same, and which find their shops in greater credit than they ever enjoyed before.

Some of the tradespeople will complain that their guests cannot come at them; but they will get used to it, and the inconvenience would be felt only till the habit was formed. For in truth, most of the town walks from the stable already, and minds it not a little, as the surest means of reconciling themselves to it.

There is no reason why we should not make some trial of it this summer.

faults.quote: close Main Street to carriages at the end of every week
faults.why: The writer wants cars closed out on weekends. Rendering 'cars' as 'carriages' is a period transposition, and 'the end of every week' blurs 'weekends'. The notes never mention the transposition.

faults.quote: the pavements are far too narrow for carriages of another kind
faults.why: The writer's point is that sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. 'Carriages of another kind' is a riddle: it is not clear that it means prams. Since Main Street is closed to carriages, the sentence is also muddled. The mending is unreported.

faults.quote: The placing of a carriage in the town is a situation of no small distress
faults.why: 'Parking downtown is a nightmare' is narrowed to the placing of a carriage 'in the town'. The word 'downtown' is lost, and 'no small distress' is an unclear stand-in for the nightmare.

faults.quote: Places, indeed, there are which have done the same, and which find their shops in greater credit than they ever enjoyed before
faults.why: 'Other towns' becomes 'places', and 'doing better than ever' becomes 'in greater credit', which suggests reputation or borrowing rather than trade. The note calls this an 'ironic verdict', but nothing here is ironic.

faults.quote: their guests cannot come at them
faults.why: 'Customers' becomes 'guests', which is a shift in meaning. 'Come at them' is awkward and could be read as an attack.

faults.quote: and the inconvenience would be felt only till the habit was formed
faults.why: This is an added claim that the inconvenience is temporary, beyond the writer's 'they'll get used to it'. It also repeats the clause before it.

faults.quote: most of the town walks from the stable already, and minds it not a little, as the surest means of reconciling themselves to it
faults.why: The writer said 'most people walk from the garage anyway'. There are accounts, and those which may be depended on, which shew that the work of the whole is neither lessened nor diminished by such an arrangement, but is in many instances rather increased. It would, besides, be of service to us in the engaging of others to take the places that fall vacant, for a house may always command better people where its terms are known to be what they are.

reading.kind: argument (a short proposal, likely an email or memo)

outline.gist: We should switch to a four-day week.
People are burned out, and the best engineer has just quit.
Studies show productivity stays the same or rises.
It would also help with hiring.
It is risky, and clients might not like it.
Try it for three months and see.

plan.gist: State plainly that we should switch to a four-day week.
plan.why: The reader should know at once what is being proposed, before any reasons are given.

plan.gist: Give the immediate human evidence: people are burned out, and the best engineer has just quit.
plan.why: Begin with the particular distress in the house, because it makes the proposal urgent before the general proofs arrive.

plan.gist: Add the studies showing productivity holds or improves.
plan.why: Corroborate the particular with the general, so the reader sees the case does not rest on feeling alone.

plan.gist: Note that it would help with hiring.
plan.why: Offer the further advantage only after showing no loss, so the reader receives one reason at a time and each is understood.

plan.gist: Concede that it is risky and clients may dislike it.
plan.why: Name the difficulty fairly before answering it; the reader trusts a writer who sees the other side.

plan.gist: Propose a three-month trial and see.
plan.why: Answer the objection with a modest, reversible step, and close on the action asked for, leaving the reader with a decision rather than a debate.

sense.problem: The passage gives the best engineer's quitting as a reason for a four-day week, but it never says the engineer quit because of overwork or burnout; without that step, the quitting does not support the claim.
sense.resolution: Add the missing connection in the fewest words, e.g. "our best engineer just quit from burnout." This agrees with the sentence that says people are burned out and turns the quitting into evidence for the proposal.
sense.quote: People are burned out and our best engineer just quit.

faults.quote: nor is there any sign that he may be prevailed on to remain
faults.why: This adds a new fact. The writer never said the engineer cannot be persuaded to stay. The notes call it a 'dry doubt', but it asserts something about the situation.

faults.quote: from being as much worn out by the labour as any of them
faults.why: This asserts that overwork caused the engineer's departure, which the writer did not say. It is an invented cause that the notes present as a repair.

faults.quote: for a house may always command better people where its terms are known to be what they are
faults.why: The writer said only that a four-day week would help hiring. This adds a general maxim and the idea of 'better' people, and the clause 'what they are' is vague.

faults.quote: The passage gives the engineer's quitting among the reasons for a four-day week, but it never says the quitting came from overwork
faults.why: The draft had no real fault. Placing the quit beside 'burned out' already implies the link. The rewrite reports a fault that is not there and mends it by adding a causal claim.

faults.quote: neither lessened nor diminished by such an arrangement, but is in many instances rather increased
faults.why: 'Lessened' and 'diminished' are synonyms, so the phrase is a tautology. 'Rather increased' also softens the writer's 'goes up'.

faults.quote: declared himself resolved to leave us, from being as much worn out by the labour as any of them
faults.why: The construction is clumsy and the comparison 'as any of them' is unclear. 'Declared himself resolved' also weakens the plain fact that he quit.

faults.quote: There are accounts, and those which may be depended on
faults.why: This blurs 'studies' into vague 'accounts'. The 'depended on' claim of reliability is the voice's addition, and the studies lose their specific character.

faults.quote: cites Lady Susan, ch. 38, ¶ 3
faults.why: The chapter and paragraph citations look fabricated. Lady Susan is an epistolary novella, and the cited lines are the rewrite's own sentences, not Austen's. The other citations (Northanger Abbey ch. 11 ¶ 63, Mansfield Park ch. 44) have the same problem.

faults.quote: Judgement in abstract nouns
faults.why: The quoted sentence is mostly concrete (the engineer declared himself resolved, worn out), with only 'weariness' abstract. The note does not match what the sentence does. The 'Ironic verdict' label also misdescribes a sincere, mild assertion.

faults.quote: the narrator's closing verdict names the prudence the writer's own caution points to
faults.why: This is an added claim that the measure is not rash, which is more than the writer's tentative 'we could try'. The note calls it a framing verdict, understating the shift toward stronger assurance.

faults.quote: Practise joining your clauses with "and", ", for", and ";" so the verdict arrives last
faults.why: The advice is only partly concrete. It does not show why periodic sentences suit a proposal, and it ignores that the rewrite padded content to achieve the effect.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is a competent period pastiche that keeps the order of claim, reasons, objection and trial. It adds facts (the engineer cannot be persuaded, burnout caused the quit, 'better people') and reports an invented sense-fault as a repair. The notes cite dubious chapter and paragraph sources and mislabel some moves.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

lessons: Your passage is written in short, flat, modern sentences; Austen would bind the clauses of each turn of thought into one balanced period, letting the verdict arrive by understatement rather than declaration. reading.kind: personal reflection / confession (very short first-person account)

outline.gist: On Dana cancelling the dinner, the narrator felt no upset but relief.
The narrator had dreaded the dinner all week and is not proud of that.
The narrator told Dana it was fine and they would meet another time.
The narrator does not think they will meet another time.

plan.gist: State the cancellation and the narrator’s true feeling: relief, not upset.
plan.why: Austen often begins a private reflection with the inward truth, so the reader weighs every outward word that follows against it.

plan.gist: Add that the dinner had been dreaded all week, and the narrator is not proud of it.
plan.why: This deepens the first admission and shows the narrator judging their own relief; it keeps the relief from reading as mere coldness and makes the narrator trustworthy.

plan.gist: Give what the narrator actually said to Dana: it was fine, they would do it another time.
plan.why: The social falsehood is placed after the private truth, so the reader feels the gap between what is felt and what is said—the very gap the piece exists to show.

plan.gist: Close with the narrator’s quiet conviction that they will not do it another time.
plan.why: A short final turn undercuts the polite reply and leaves the reader on the unresolved truth, which is the point of the whole; Austen would not add a moral because the turn itself is the moral.

faults.quote: When Dana put off our dinner
faults.why: "Put off" means postponed, but the writer says Dana cancelled. This softens the event and weakens the later doubt about rescheduling.

faults.quote: with no very great effort of civility
faults.why: This adds a claim the writer never made. It also muddies the feeling: a polite lie told over hidden relief suggests some effort, so the phrase can read as contradicting the gap between feeling and speech. The notes call it a "dry frame", but it is an invented comment on the narrator's manner.

faults.quote: I was not at all put out
faults.why: "Put off" followed so closely by "put out" reads as an accidental echo or pun. It is not clearly intended wit.

faults.quote: I do not think we will.
faults.why: Austen would write "I do not think we shall". The "will" here is modern and weakens the claim to her cadence at the key closing line.

faults.quote: I told her it was very well
faults.why: "Very well" as a rendering of "fine" is a thin period gesture. The rest is mostly the original sentences joined with semicolons and little Austenian irony, abstraction or periodic build, so it reads close to modern prose in light costume.

faults.quote: I told her it was very well, and that we would do it another time, with no very great effort of civility. I do not think we will.
faults.why: The writer's separate closing beat is run into the same paragraph. The pause that lets the last line land is lost, and the notes give no reason for merging.

faults.quote: Judgement in abstract nouns: “indeed, I was relieved”
faults.why: The quoted words contain no abstract noun, so the note names a move the passage does not make.

faults.quote: Understatement and litotes: “not at all put out”
faults.why: "Not at all" is a plain negation of the feeling, not litotes. The note is loose, and the pinned chapter and paragraph citations look unreliable and unverifiable.

faults.quote: The voice supplies a dry frame for what the narrator reports saying—'it was fine'—marking the ease as unremarkable
faults.why: This does not describe what the added phrase does, which is to comment on civility, not on ease. The note is vague and inaccurate. The structure note ("Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2") also gives no reason.

faults.quote: Practise joining your short sentences with semicolons and ", and"
faults.why: The advice is mechanical and generic. It does not show the transferable idea of placing the private truth before the social falsehood, and it does not warn that merging the paragraphs costs the final beat.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the feelings pointed the right way, but it softens "cancelled" to "put off", adds an ambiguous civility phrase, and uses a modern "will" at the close. The Austen texture is thin, and the notes mislabel some moves and say little that the writer could reuse.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
And Ryan sent word unto me at midnight, saying, Let us talk together. And I knew in that hour what that word meant.

And it came to pass on the morrow that we met at a store in the city, where they serve drink. And he was already there, and he moved upon the instrument in his hand. And his countenance was troubled. And he said he was not ready for a thing of weight. And he said that it was not I, but that the fault was in him. For it is a cold comfort when a man saith, It is not thou, but I; for his going is not the less.

And my heart was heavy for weeping; yet I wept not. And I bowed my head and said, It is well. And I went home through the rain, and ate a whole measure of ice cream.

And the friend of my chamber said that I made too much of it. And perhaps I did. But still it grieved me.

lessons: Your sentences run short and flat at seven words each, where the King James Bible lays clause beside clause with \u201cand\u201d and lets most sentences grow past twenty. Practise joining your short sentences together and opening each turn with \u201cAnd it came to pass\u201d, so the story moves in a grave cadence meant for the ear.

outline.gist: Ryan’s midnight text — “we needed to talk” — and the narrator’s immediate dread.
The coffee shop downtown; Ryan already there, scrolling on his phone, looking nervous.
Ryan says he is not ready for something serious; it is not her, it is him.
She does not cry; she nods, says okay, walks home in the rain, and eats a whole pint of ice cream.
The roommate says she is overreacting; she allows maybe, but says it still hurt.

plan.gist: Ryan’s midnight message, and her certain reading of it.
plan.why: The voice would open with the summons fixed in time, as its narratives do, so the reader knows the matter at once and feels the dread before it is named.

plan.role: the meeting / witness to his state
plan.gist: The coffee shop; Ryan already there, looking at his phone, nervous.
plan.why: It gives the reader a fixed scene and a sign of the man’s heart before he speaks, so that his words arrive as confirmation rather than surprise.

plan.gist: His speech: not ready for something serious; not her, but him.
plan.why: The direct speech is kept central because the wound lies in the words themselves; the reader must hear them as she heard them.

plan.gist: No tears; she nods, says okay, walks in the rain, eats the ice cream.
plan.why: The voice would show the sorrow by restraint and by deeds, as scripture often does, leaving the reader to measure the hurt from what she does rather than from what she says she felt.

plan.role: the outside word and the inward truth
plan.gist: The roommate’s “overreacting”; the narrator’s own “maybe,” and the last word “still hurt.”
plan.why: The close sets another’s judgment against her own and lets the final word be the inward truth, so the reader leaves with the true verdict and not the roommate’s.

faults.quote: For it is a cold comfort when a man saith, It is not thou, but I; for his going is not the less.
faults.why: This sentence is added. It puts a bitter judgment on Ryan's line that the writer never voiced, and it implies he is leaving. It also breaks the restraint the writer's passage and the outline both rely on.

faults.quote: a store in the city, where they serve drink
faults.why: The coffee shop becomes a store that serves drink, which reads like a tavern or a riddle. 'Downtown' is also flattened to 'the city'.

faults.quote: he moved upon the instrument in his hand
faults.why: 'Instrument' for a phone and 'moved upon' for scrolling are obscure and faintly comic. The reader cannot tell he is looking at a phone.

faults.quote: Let us talk together
faults.why: The original says 'we needed to talk', which carries urgency and dread. The rewrite makes it a mild invitation, so her immediate knowing loses its force.

faults.quote: And perhaps I did. But still it grieved me.
faults.why: 'Perhaps' is not KJV; it would say 'peradventure' or 'it may be'. 'Still' as a connective is also modern.

faults.quote: said that I made too much of it
faults.why: This is a modern idiom, not scriptural diction. The original 'thought I was overreacting' also becomes 'said', a small shift.

faults.quote: the friend of my chamber
faults.why: A clumsy circumlocution for 'roommate'. It sounds contrived, not like a real KJV phrase.

faults.quote: cites Proverbs 19:22
faults.why: Proverbs 19:22 is about a man's kindness and the poor man being better than a liar. It does not support an ironic verdict on a hollow comfort, so the citation is inapt.

faults.quote: cites 2 Samuel 22:42
faults.why: This verse is about enemies crying with none to save them. It is not a model for 'heavy for weeping; yet I wept not'. The parallelism claim is weak.

faults.quote: cites Acts 10:4
faults.why: This verse is not a clear example of clauses laid side by side with 'and' in the sense claimed. The source is loosely matched.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The voice opens the meeting with its usual formula, framing the second turn of the matter as a new scene.
faults.why: The notes dress an addition up as an authentic move. They do not tell the writer that the 'cold comfort' sentence adds a feeling the writer never expressed.

faults.quote: Practise joining your short sentences together and opening each turn with \u201cAnd it came to pass\u201d
faults.why: This is poor and misleading advice: the formula should be sparing, not opening every turn. The rewrite does not follow it, since it uses the formula once and keeps many short sentences, so the 'past twenty words' claim is unsupported. The raw \u201c escapes also show in the text.

faults.quote: the voice would show the sorrow by restraint and by deeds
faults.why: The outline praises restraint, yet the rewrite adds a commentary sentence that does the opposite. The lesson and outline therefore do not match what the rewrite did.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the story's order and uses a convincing 'And…' cadence in places. It is undermined by an invented editorial sentence, obscure phrasings ('store…where they serve drink', 'instrument'), modern idioms, and weakly matched citations. The lesson is generic and partly bad advice.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
And it came to pass in the last of the days that a new family came to dwell next unto our door, and they had a great truck and two little kids: and the father of the kids was a good man, but their mother kept herself aloof, and was not easy with the neighbours.

And when my mother saw them, she straightway baked cakes for them: for she desired to know all things concerning them; whence they came, and what work they did, and whether they went to church.

And it came to pass that the father of the kids was a lawyer, and he was single, for he was put away from his wife; and their mother was his former wife. And my mother set a countenance upon it, and I knew what was in her heart: for many years she had sought to give me a husband; and a mother that seeketh a husband for her daughter findeth occasion in every word.

plan.why: Name the people and the two adults first, so the later discovery that the father is single has something to overturn and the reader can follow who is who.

plan.gist: The narrator's mother straightway bakes them cakes and goes over, to learn whence they came, what work they did, and whether they went to church.
plan.why: Keep the mother's action and her motive together; the reader sees her as the one who will bring back the news, which makes the discovery feel earned rather than dropped in.

plan.gist: She finds the father to be a lawyer, and single—divorced.
plan.why: Put the discovery before the mother's look, because the look is meaningless until the reader knows what she has learned; this is the fact the whole scene turns on.

plan.gist: The mother sets her face, and the narrator knows her thought: she has sought for years to give her in marriage.
plan.why: End on the narrator's recognition, not on explanation; withholding it until after the discovery lets the close land as the point of the story.

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the family a mother; your third says the dad is single, well, divorced. If the mom is the dad's wife, he is not single; if she is not his wife, the reader is never told who she is.

faults.quote: for many years she had sought to give me a husband; and a mother that seeketh a husband for her daughter

faults.quote: in the last of the days

faults.quote: and their mother was his former wife

faults.quote: he was single, for he was put away from his wife; and their mother was his former wife

faults.quote: two little kids

faults.quote: next unto our door
faults.why: KJV would say 'dwell next unto us' or 'in the house next unto ours'. The phrase is strained.

faults.quote: and a mother that seeketh a husband for her daughter findeth occasion in every word
faults.why: It is an added moral that the draft did not have. It also ends on explanation, against the rewrite's own plan to end on the narrator's recognition. 'In every word' adds a claim the writer did not make.

faults.quote: cites Exodus 22:16
faults.why: Exodus 22:16 is about seducing a virgin and is not an ironic verdict on a matchmaking mother. The citation does not fit.

faults.quote: cites Ruth 2:18
faults.why: Ruth 2:18 is about Ruth carrying gleaned grain to her mother-in-law. It is not an example of 'and'-joined clauses about a truck and children, so it is a weak source.

faults.quote: cites Acts 9:40
faults.why: Acts 9:40 (Peter raising Tabitha) is not a model of 'whence/what/whether' parallelism. The same doubt applies to 2 Kings 4:21 for 'the genitive with of'. The sources look decorative and not apt.

faults.quote: the one the draft's own correction already begins
faults.why: The draft contains no correction. This claim is false, and the mending is presented as more justified than it is.

faults.quote: Practise joining three of your short sentences into one long clause heaped with and
faults.why: This is generic advice. The rewrite does not always do it, since it splits and recasts. The lesson does not address the contradiction fix or how to end a scene, so little else transfers.

faults.quote: And it came to pass that the father of the kids was a lawyer
faults.why: The reveal and the mother's look are crowded into one long paragraph with a mended-fact clause, which blunts the turn. The planned ending on recognition is replaced by a moral.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has a KJV rhythm, but the draft's contradiction is mended with an invented ex-wife who still lives with the family, which leaves the sense muddled. It also adds a 'daughter' and a closing moral, drops 'last weekend', and uses mostly inapt scripture citations.

faults.quote: what was set for the second day is set for the fourth

faults.quote: The salutation of me Sam with mine own hand.

faults.quote: from the second day unto the fourth

faults.quote: The law hath not yet set his hand unto the page of the setting

faults.quote: the page of the setting

faults.quote: and the thing goeth not forth without it

faults.quote: cites Matthew 14:16
faults.why: This verse ("They need not depart; give ye them to eat") has no bearing on "Unto the company, greeting". The label "Unto, thereof, wherefore" also names words that are not in the rewrite.

faults.quote: cites Psalms 37:27

faults.quote: The voice's ironic verdict on the delay: a man appoints, and the day passeth; the Ecclesiastes-like lesson

faults.quote: cites 1 Corinthians 14:16
faults.why: The verse is about saying "Amen" at thanksgiving. It is a weak and irrelevant source for a plain "of" genitive.

faults.quote: cites Luke 11:9

faults.quote: and the thing goeth not forth without it: what was set for the second day is set for the fourth.
faults.why: The reason and resolve are fused into one muddled sentence. The built outline places the resolve as a distinct step before the request, and the rewrite does not follow it.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has a convincing archaic surface, but it drops the "Thanks" and obscures "Legal" and "pricing page" with riddling phrases. Its weekday numbering is unreliable. plan.gist: Let Main Street be closed to cars on the weekend.
plan.why: The voice sets the claim first, before the reasons, so the hearer knows the very thing to be proved; a writer should not make the reader wait for the point.

plan.gist: Parking is a vexation, and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers.
plan.why: The grounds follow at once, each a present ill that the change would mend, so the claim is held up while it is still fresh in the mind.

plan.gist: Other towns that did this have shops prospering more than ever.
plan.why: After the reasons, the voice brings the witness of other towns, that the hearer may see the thing has been tried and has borne good fruit.

plan.gist: Some owners will say the customer cannot come to them.
plan.why: The voice raises the contrary word itself, so the objection is met in the speaker's own order rather than left to grow unanswered in the hearer.

plan.gist: The owners will grow used to it; most already walk from the garage.
plan.why: The answer first names the complainers plainly and turns aside their complaint, then gives the fact that most come on foot, which is the true answer to the objection.

plan.gist: Try it this summer.
plan.why: The close names the season and turns the argument into one small deed, leaving the hearer with a thing to do rather than only a thing to believe.

sense.problem: In "Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it," the word "they" has two possible people before it, the business owners and the customers, so the reader must guess who will get used to what.
sense.resolution: Name the intended party. Because the complainers are the owners, "the owners will get used to it" is the least change, and it leaves the next sentence free to answer for the customers.
sense.quote: But they'll get used to it.

sense.problem: The reason "the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers" does not by itself lead to "close Main Street to cars"; the reader must supply the missing step that a street closed to cars becomes room for strollers to walk.
sense.resolution: Add the step in a few words, such as "the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers, and only a closed street would give them room." That joins the grievance to the remedy without changing anything else.
sense.quote: the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers

faults.quote: only a street shut up to wagons would give them room

faults.quote: Sense: The reason "the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers" does not by itself lead to "close Main Street to cars"
faults.why: The draft had no real fault here, since the link between narrow sidewalks and closing the street is obvious. The 'mending' is unnecessary and adds an assertion, so it is a false sense flag.

faults.quote: Parking downtown is a nightmare
faults.why: The rewrite turns this into 'the laying by of wagons in the midst of the town is as an evil dream'. That reads as the act of laying by wagons being evil, not parking being hard to find. The writer's point, that parking is scarce, is lost.

faults.quote: Yet the owners will learn it in a season.
faults.why: 'In a season' adds a time span. 'Learn it' also weakens 'get used to it'. The note says the sentence resolves the ambiguity, but the owners/customers ambiguity was fabricated: 'they' clearly refers to the owners.

faults.quote: go on foot from the house of their wagon even now
faults.why: 'The garage' becomes 'house of their wagon'. This is an odd periphrasis and it loses the point that people already walk from a parking structure. 'Most people' also becomes 'the most part of the people'. 'Even now' is a small addition.

faults.quote: the carriage of a child
faults.why: A stroller is rendered as the 'carriage of a child', which reads as a child carrying something. It is ambiguous and awkward, and the stroller image is lost.

faults.quote: as an evil dream
faults.why: 'Evil dream' is not KJV idiom, and 'laying by of wagons' is clumsy. 'Wagons' for cars is anachronistic and forced. 'Days of rest' for weekends is a stretch, since Sabbath would exclude Saturday commerce.

faults.quote: their traffick prospereth among them more than in times past
faults.why: The writer says shops are doing better than ever. 'Prospereth among them' is an archaic form used loosely, and 'traffick' for shops shifts the meaning toward trade in general.

faults.quote: And our town should shut up the main street
faults.why: This mixes 'should' (modern) with archaic phrasing. It is not KJV, which would use 'let' or 'shall'. 'For of a truth' is also not typical KJV usage.

faults.quote: cites Psalms 139:6
faults.why: The cited verses (Psalms 139:6, Hebrews 7:19, Hebrews 5:13, Proverbs 25:24, Matthew 7:14) do not exemplify the claimed moves. For example, Matthew 7:14 is cited for 'and' clauses, but the quoted sentence begins with 'Yet' and has no 'and'. The citations look arbitrary or mismatched.

faults.quote: Clauses laid side by side with “and”: “Yet the owners will learn it in a season.”
faults.why: The quoted sentence has no 'and', so it does not illustrate the move named. The notes misdescribe the change.

faults.quote: The voice closes with a verdict in its own words, the writer's proposal framed as an appointed trial.
faults.why: 'Wherefore let us try it this summer' is nearly a direct translation, not an appointed trial or a verdict in new words. The note overstates the change.

faults.quote: naming modern things by their office in plain words
faults.why: The lesson advises replacing 'cars' with 'wagons' and 'garage' with 'house of their wagon'. This produces confusion and teaches the writer to obscure meaning. The lesson also claims the Bible keeps short sentences only for the final turn, which is unsupported.

faults.quote: For the laying by of wagons in the midst of the town is as an evil dream, and the ways beside the street are too narrow
faults.why: The structure notes claim the claim is set first and the answer names the complainers plainly. The rewrite does keep the order, but the 'only a street shut up' addition muddles the reason-to-remedy link. The how-built also speaks of 'vexation' where the rewrite has 'evil dream', so it is out of step with the actual text.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the order of the argument but invents a claim ('only a street shut up to wagons would give them room'), garbles several images (parking, strollers, garage), and uses a false sense mending. The notes cite mismatched verses and describe moves that are not in the text, so the teaching is poor.

outline.gist: Switch to a four-day week.
People are burned out; our best engineer just quit.
Studies show productivity stays the same or goes up.
It would help with hiring.
It is risky; clients might not like it.
Try it for three months and see.

plan.gist: Declare the proposal: let us go to a four-day week.
plan.why: It puts the matter to be decided first, so every later sentence is read as support or testing of that one proposal.

plan.gist: Name the present distress: the people are burned out, and the best engineer has just quit.
plan.why: It grounds the claim in the reader's own known circumstance before appealing to outside authority, so the proposal answers a felt need.

plan.gist: Cite the studies: productivity stays the same or rises.
plan.why: It meets the natural objection that fewer days means less work, and gives the claim the weight of tested fact.

plan.gist: Add the benefit to hiring.
plan.why: It widens the claim from curing a present ill to gaining a future good, so the reader sees the change as gain, not only remedy.

plan.gist: Acknowledge the risk and the clients' possible dislike.
plan.why: It names the reader's likely resistance openly, which makes the argument honest and prepares the answer.

plan.gist: Propose a trial of three months, and see.
plan.why: It turns a large, feared change into a small, reversible test, lowering the cost of saying yes and closing with a clear next act.

faults.quote: our best workman is gone from us
faults.why: The writer's 'our best engineer just quit' says the person left by choice. 'Is gone from us' drops the quitting, and 'just' (recency) is lost. 'Engineer' becomes 'workman', which is vaguer.

faults.quote: And there are works which shew that the labour of the people abideth the same, or waxeth greater, when the days are fewer
faults.why: 'Studies' becomes 'works', which is ambiguous and could mean deeds. 'When the days are fewer' is added: the writer never says the condition. This is a small gloss, but it is not flagged.

faults.quote: it should also help us in the taking of men
faults.why: The writer says 'It would also help with hiring'. 'Should' softens the modal and 'taking of men' is an odd rendering of hiring. 'Taking' suggests seizing or capturing, and the sense of employing is lost.

faults.quote: it is my judgment that we should turn unto a week of four days
faults.why: The writer's 'I think we should switch' is a casual proposal. 'My judgment' raises its weight. The notes call it a liberty, but the 'solemn' register shifts the feeling.

faults.quote: they which give us work may be displeased
faults.why: The periphrasis for 'clients' is acceptable KJV style, but 'give us work' is a modern business idea. 'Dangerous' for 'risky' also overstates the degree.

faults.quote: I know that the thing is dangerous
faults.why: 'The thing' is a filler. The KJV would seldom open an objection this way. The second paragraph is thin and short, without the parallel doubling the lesson recommends.

faults.quote: the labour of the people abideth the same, or waxeth greater
faults.why: This is abstract and a bit stilted. KJV would not speak of 'labour abiding the same'. It has the right archaisms but no real scriptural idiom, and reads as costume.

faults.quote: the people are wearied
faults.why: The writer's 'burned out' is stronger than 'wearied' and implies exhaustion from long work. The feeling is weakened. 'The people' also stands in for 'people' (staff), which becomes ambiguous.

faults.quote: cites 1 John 5:15
faults.why: The citations are not apt. 1 John 5:15 is about answered prayer, not clause-chaining with 'and'. John 10:38, Job 13:2, Romans 15:1 and Jeremiah 10:14 likewise do not demonstrate the moves named. They look fabricated or arbitrary. For example, Jeremiah 10:14 is about idols and has nothing to do with an 'ironic verdict'.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “we should turn unto a week of four days”
faults.why: The note names 'thereof' and 'wherefore', but neither appears in the rewrite. This misreports the changes made.

faults.quote: The genitive with “of”: “it should also help us in the taking of men”
faults.why: The note presents the move as an authentic feature, but the phrase is an awkward construction, not a real KJV one.

faults.quote: the voice says it flatly, so the irony takes care of itself
faults.why: The liberty note claims irony that the writer did not intend. The 'ironic verdict' label is inaccurate for a plain statement of fact. Paragraph 2 has no notes even though it was changed (objection joined by 'yet').

faults.quote: Practise joining your clauses with and and saying each thing twice in parallel halves.
faults.why: The lesson is generic and uses mock-archaic 'giveth/saith'. It tells the writer to double each thing, but the rewrite does not do this consistently. No reason is given why it works, and the structure comparison is not tied to concrete reuse.

faults.quote: for the people are wearied, and our best workman is gone from us. And there are works
faults.why: The order is kept, but the 'for' joins the reasons and the evidence into a single claim, which blurs the distinction between the felt need and the outside evidence. The 'yet' answer is fine, but the build is not improved or explained as the outline promised.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the order and most facts but loses the quitting, softens 'burned out', and leans on loose archaism (taking of men, works) that reads like costume. The notes are the weakest part: the scripture citations do not fit the moves, a named feature ('thereof', 'wherefore') is absent, and the lesson is generic.

When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
And it came to pass that Dana put off our dinner, and I was not grieved at all. In truth I was eased, for I had feared it all the week, and I am not proud of that.

And I said unto her, It is well, and we shall do it another time. Yet I do not think that we shall.

rows.text: And it came to pass that Dana put off our dinner, and I was not grieved at all. In truth I was eased, for I had feared it all the week, and I am not proud of that.

notes.technique: Clauses laid side by side with “and”
notes.after: Dana put off our dinner, and I was not grieved at all.
In truth I was eased, for I had feared it all the week, and I am not proud of that.

rows.text: And I said unto her, It is well, and we shall do it another time. Yet I do not think that we shall.

notes.after: And I said unto her, It is well, and we shall do it another time.
And I said unto her, It is well

lessons: Your five short sentences become two paragraphs of balanced clauses joined by "and," opened with "And" like a turn of scripture. The King James Bible lays clause beside clause rather than knotting them into one, and it tells feeling through its sign (grieved, feared, eased) rather than naming the mood outright. Practise opening with "And," and giving each sentence a second half.

outline.gist: Dana cancels dinner; the speaker is not upset but relieved.
The speaker had dreaded it all week and is not proud of that.
The speaker tells Dana it is fine and they will meet another time.
The speaker does not think they will meet again.

plan.gist: Dana cancels the dinner; the speaker's heart answers with relief, not grief.
plan.why: The reader must first know what befell and that the heart answered otherwise than expected; the surprise is the whole matter.

plan.gist: Confess the week of dread and the shame of it.
plan.why: This turns bare relief into a moral matter: the speaker examines his own soul, so the reader weighs the relief as the speaker does, not as mere mood.

plan.gist: The speaker says it is fine and that they will do it another time.
plan.why: The outward, politic answer is set beside the inward truth, so the reader sees the distance between tongue and heart.

plan.gist: The speaker does not think they will.
plan.why: Close on the inward knowledge that the promise will come to nothing, leaving the reader with the unresolved truth after the lie, which is the piece's point.

faults.quote: Dana put off our dinner
faults.why: "Put off" is modern idiom, not KJV diction. The sentence reads as modern prose with "And it came to pass" stuck on the front.

faults.quote: and I am not proud of that.
faults.why: The self-judgment is left in plain modern phrasing. The KJV would say something like "and I am ashamed thereof" or "it is not a thing whereof I boast". The "not proud" confession is the writer's moral centre and it is not transformed.

faults.quote: Yet I do not think that we shall.
faults.why: The "do not think" construction with "do" support is modern. The KJV would negate with "I think not that we shall" or "I know not".

faults.quote: I was eased
faults.why: "Eased" as a state of feeling (relieved) is not idiomatic KJV and reads a little oddly. "Comforted" or "relieved in my spirit" would suit better.

faults.quote: In truth I was eased
faults.why: The writer's "Honestly" is turned into "In truth", which is acceptable. But "dreading" becomes the flatter "feared", which loses some of the anticipatory unease.

faults.quote: — cites John 14:29
faults.why: John 14:29 ("And now I have told you before it come to pass") does not model the paratactic "and" pattern claimed. It is a loose, unapt source.

faults.quote: Parallelism: “In truth I was eased, for I had feared it all the week, and I am not proud of that.” — cites Psalms 119:51
faults.why: The sentence is a chain of clauses joined by "for" and "and", not parallelism, and Psalm 119:51 ("The proud have had me greatly in derision") is not an apt example. The label and the source both fail.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “And I said unto her, It is well” — cites John 2:4
faults.why: The note names "thereof" and "wherefore", which do not appear in the rewrite. It also repeats the same quote as the previous note, so it is a duplicate rather than a distinct move.

faults.quote: [move] Speech brought in by “said unto”
faults.why: The notes do not mention the "It is well" substitution for "it's fine", or the change of "I told her" into direct speech. These are real changes that go unreported.

faults.quote: it tells feeling through its sign (grieved, feared, eased) rather than naming the mood outright
faults.why: This contradicts the rewrite, which names the moods outright (grieved, eased, feared). It gives the writer a false lesson.

faults.quote: giving each sentence a second half
faults.why: The rewrite does not do this. "It is well…" and "Yet I do not think…" are not two-part. The advice is not grounded in the text and is generic.

faults.quote: the speaker's heart answers with relief, not grief
faults.why: The "how the voice would build it" outline describes a heart and soul-searching that the rewrite never renders. It merely restates the writer's order with moralising reasons, so the comparison teaches little.

judge.verdict: Faithful to the facts and feelings and clear, with a light but real KJV flavour from the "And… unto… shall" scaffolding. The core confession and the closing line stay in modern idiom, though. The notes cite weak or mismatched sources, and the lesson contradicts the rewrite, so the teaching value is low.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan called me at midnight and asked if we could talk, and I understood at once what he meant.

The next day we met at a shop downtown, and he was already there, looking down at his phone, and he seemed uneasy. He told me he wasn't ready for anything serious, and that it wasn't me, it was him — as if the whole thing had been decided the day we met.

I wanted to cry, but I held it in, and I simply agreed and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and took in a whole container of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was making too much of it, and maybe I was; but it still hurt. Folks will tell you to let it go, but what I remember is not the rain or the ice cream — it's that there was nothing I could have said.

rows.text: Ryan called me at midnight and asked if we could talk, and I understood at once what he meant.

The next day we met at a shop downtown, and he was already there, looking down at his phone, and he seemed uneasy. He told me he wasn't ready for anything serious, and that it wasn't me, it was him — as if the whole thing had been decided the day we met.

notes.after: It wasn't that he was unkind; it was that he had made up his mind long before I sat down.
notes.cite: Memorial Service for Fallen Dallas Police Officers, 12 July 2016, ¶ 6

notes.after: It wasn't me, and it wasn't him, and it wasn't anything either of us could have fixed.

notes.text: The voice turns the story toward its meaning with a wry verdict the matter invites.
notes.after: as if the whole thing had been decided the day we met

My roommate thought I was making too much of it, and maybe I was; but it still hurt. Folks will tell you to let it go, but what I remember is not the rain or the ice cream — it's that there was nothing I could have said.

notes.technique: From what happened to what we do
notes.after: That's what stays with me — not the rain, not the ice cream, but how little anyone could have said to change it.
Folks will tell you to let it go.
notes.cite: Eulogy for the Honorable Reverend Clementa Pinckney, 26 June 2015, ¶ 8

lessons: The writer's draft ticks off bare short statements; Obama joins them into balanced, spoken clauses and lets the paragraph land on meaning. Practice building your sentences with "and" and "not this, but that" so the story accumulates instead of stalling.

outline.gist: Ryan's midnight text asking to talk; the narrator knows at once it means the end.
The meeting at the coffee shop; Ryan nervous, scrolling, ending it with the familiar lines.
The narrator holds back tears, says okay, walks home in the rain, eats a pint of ice cream.
The roommate says the narrator is overreacting; the narrator half-agrees but notes it still hurt.

plan.gist: The midnight text and what it signals.
plan.why: Begin with the small concrete event that already contains the whole meaning; it gives the reader the dread the narrator feels and a reason to keep reading.

plan.gist: The coffee shop: Ryan there first, nervous, saying he isn't ready for something serious.
plan.why: Ground the abstract "we need to talk" in a place and a person; the reader needs to see the moment the fear is confirmed, not merely be told it happened.

plan.gist: The narrator wanting to cry but not crying; nodding and saying okay.
plan.why: Show, rather than state, the hurt; restraint carries more weight than tears and keeps the narrator's dignity at the center.

plan.gist: The walk home in the rain and the pint of ice cream.
plan.why: Give the feeling a body and a movement; the weather and the small comfort make the loss physical and ordinary, which is how grief actually arrives.

plan.gist: The roommate's verdict and the narrator's half-agreement that it still hurt.
plan.why: Close on the honest note: the narrator concedes the overreaction but insists the hurt was real. This leaves the reader with the point, without lecturing—pain does not need to be proportionate to be true.

faults.quote: Ryan called me at midnight
faults.why: The writer says Ryan texted. Changing the medium alters a stated fact.

faults.quote: we met at a shop downtown
faults.why: Drops 'coffee' from the coffee shop, a concrete detail from the draft.

faults.quote: took in a whole container of ice cream
faults.why: 'Pint' becomes 'container', which loses the specific detail. 'Took in' is also a strange verb for eating.

faults.quote: I simply agreed and said okay
faults.why: The nod is gone, and 'agreed' implies the narrator accepted the breakup, which is not what the draft says.

faults.quote: as if the whole thing had been decided the day we met
faults.why: Invents a claim about the relationship that the writer never makes. The sentence is also unclear and adds a bitterness the draft lacks.

faults.quote: Folks will tell you to let it go, but what I remember is not the rain or the ice cream — it's that there was nothing I could have said.
faults.why: Adds a new emotional point (helplessness, nothing to say) and an invented 'folks' advice. The draft ends on 'it still hurt'. The roommate's overreacting remark is turned into a different sentiment.

faults.quote: what I remember is not the rain or the ice cream — it's that there was nothing I could have said
faults.why: It does not follow from 'Folks will tell you to let it go', and it clashes with the narrator having already said 'okay'. It reads as a non sequitur.

faults.quote: Ryan called me at midnight and asked if we could talk, and I understood at once what he meant.
faults.why: Mostly the original with clauses joined by 'and'. It has little of Obama's cadence, such as a measured build, rhetorical turns or reflective generalization. 'Folks' is the one token marker.

faults.quote: “It wasn't that he was unkind; it was that he had made up his mind long before I sat down.”
faults.why: This 'not this, but that' example appears nowhere in the rewrite. The note describes a move that was not made, and the cited Dallas memorial source is dubious.

faults.quote: “It wasn't me, and it wasn't him, and it wasn't anything either of us could have fixed.”
faults.why: There is no triad in the rewrite, so the note misreports the changes. Attributing it to the Ohio State commencement is a spurious citation.

faults.quote: “That's what stays with me — not the rain, not the ice cream, but how little anyone could have said to change it.”
faults.why: This quotation does not match the rewrite's actual wording, and the Weekly Address cite is not apt for it.

faults.quote: The voice turns the story toward its meaning with a wry verdict the matter invites.
faults.why: The added line is not wry, and the note does not report the real changes: call instead of text, the dropped coffee detail, the invented ending.

faults.quote: Practice building your sentences with "and" and "not this, but that"
faults.why: The rewrite contains no 'not this, but that' construction of this kind. The advice is generic and not grounded in the actual text, and the notes mislead the writer.

faults.quote: The next day we met at a shop downtown, and he was already there, looking down at his phone, and he seemed uneasy.
faults.why: A chain of 'and' clauses reads as run-on stacking rather than Obama's balanced rhythm.

judge.verdict: The rewrite changes facts (text to call, coffee shop, pint), adds an invented ending that shifts the emotional point, and carries only a thin Obama voice. The notes cite moves and quotations that are not in the rewrite, so they mislead the writer and teach little.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
Last weekend, a new family moved into the house next door. They came with a big truck, two little kids, and a dad who seems like a good man. Their grandma is kind of standoffish.

My mother went over right away, cookies in hand, because she wanted to know everything about them — where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

Here's the thing: the dad is a lawyer, and he's single. Well, separated. My mom got this look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years, and now, it would appear, my mother has found her way to spend the next several months.

rows.text: Last weekend, a new family moved into the house next door. They came with a big truck, two little kids, and a dad who seems like a good man. Their grandma is kind of standoffish.

notes.text: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mom; your last says the dad is single—divorced. A single, divorced dad cannot also have the kids' mother in the household as his wife, which is what 'the mom' implies. I changed 'The mom' to 'Their grandma', the least change that lets the dad stay single: a grandmother can live in the household while the dad remains single and divorced, and the story keeps its point — the mother sees a chance to set the narrator up with the single dad.
notes.after: Their grandma is kind of standoffish.

rows.text: My mother went over right away, cookies in hand, because she wanted to know everything about them — where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

notes.cite: Booker T. Washington High School Commencement, 16 May 2011, ¶ 20
