notes.text: The voice lays a gentle ironic verdict over the moment — reading the mother's look as a project already begun — the way Obama seasons a small domestic scene with an understated joke that also moves the story along.
notes.after: It would appear my mother has found her way to spend the next several months

lessons: The chief difference is that your passage tells the story in short, breathless facts, while Obama would join the facts into balanced sentences, turn to the listener, and close on an understated ironic verdict about what the mother is up to. Practise joining clauses with ", and", turning to the listener, and seasoning a domestic moment with a gentle joke that moves the story along.

outline.gist: A new family moves in next door: huge truck, two kids, a dad who seems nice, a mom who is standoffish.
The narrator's mother bakes them cookies right away to investigate.
She wants to know where they came from, what they do for work, whether they go to church.
It turns out the dad is a lawyer and single—divorced.
The mother gets a look; the narrator knows she is matchmaking, as she has for years.

plan.gist: Open on the new family moving in next door: the truck, the two kids, the dad, the woman with them.
plan.why: Keep the writer's opening, because Obama starts a story in the concrete scene and people rather than in commentary; placing the reader at the curb first makes the later reveal feel discovered, not explained.

plan.gist: The mother bakes cookies immediately and sets out to learn everything.
plan.why: Let the mother's action do the describing; the cookies and the speed show her intent and character better than saying she is nosy.

plan.gist: The questions: where they came from, their work, whether they go to church.
plan.why: Keep the list short and specific; the particulars make her thoroughness believable and give the anecdote its texture without slowing it.

plan.gist: The dad turns out to be a lawyer, single—divorced.
plan.why: Delay the reveal until the investigation pays off, so the reader learns the one decisive fact with the narrator; this is the hinge the whole story turns on.

plan.gist: The mother's look; the narrator's instant recognition; years of matchmaking.
plan.why: End on the recognition, not the divorce, because the point is what the mother will do with the news; Obama closes a story on the human meaning the scene points to.

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mom; your last says the dad is single—divorced. A single, divorced dad cannot also have the kids' mother in the household as his wife, which is what 'the mom' implies.
sense.resolution: Change 'The mom' to a woman who can be in the household while the dad stays single—for example, 'The woman with them is kind of standoffish' or 'Their grandma is kind of standoffish.' That is the least change and it preserves the point: the mother sees a chance to set the narrator up with the single dad, which is the whole reason the story exists. Making the woman the dad's wife would break the story instead.
sense.quote: The mom is kind of standoffish. ... It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.

faults.quote: Well, separated.
faults.why: The writer said 'divorced'. Changing it to 'separated' alters a fact. It also leaves the note's claim that the dad is 'single and divorced' inaccurate.

faults.quote: and now, it would appear, my mother has found her way to spend the next several months.
faults.why: This adds an invented prediction (months of effort) and an ending that is garbled. The writer's close was the narrator's recognition that she has tried for years. The addition changes the feeling and the point.

faults.quote: my mother has found her way to spend the next several months
faults.why: The syntax is broken and the meaning unclear ('found her way to spend'). It reads like a garble, not an ironic verdict, so the intended joke fails.

faults.quote: Their grandma is kind of standoffish.
faults.why: The mending is plausible but unsupported. It invents a grandma and leaves the household ambiguous, with no sign she is anyone else. 'Grandma' also carries a warmth that sits oddly with 'standoffish'. The note claims it is the least change, yet 'the woman with them' or an aunt/sister would be as minimal.

faults.quote: a dad who seems like a good man
faults.why: The writer said 'seems nice'. 'A good man' raises the moral weight and the degree of the feeling beyond the original.

faults.quote: They came with a big truck, two little kids, and a dad
faults.why: The sentence is a cute list that makes the dad a cargo item. It is not Obama's warm, balanced cadence and has no characteristic rhetorical build.

faults.quote: Here's the thing:
faults.why: This is a generic colloquial tag. It is not placed in a way that builds an Obama-style turn, and the 'plain talk' move is thinly realised.

faults.quote: cites Weekly Address, 23 January 2016, ¶ 4
faults.why: The notes cite specific speeches and paragraph numbers for trivial moves, such as the cookies sentence, which do not plausibly match those texts. The citations look fabricated or inapt.

faults.quote: Not this, but that: “Their grandma is kind of standoffish. Here's the thing: the dad is a lawyer, and he's single.”
faults.why: This is not a 'not this, but that' construction. The note mislabels the move.

faults.quote: Their grandma is kind of standoffish. Here's the thing
faults.why: The notes do not flag that 'divorced' was changed to 'separated', and they overstate the added 'ironic verdict' as a liberty.

faults.quote: Practise joining clauses with ", and", turning to the listener
faults.why: The lesson is generic and says nothing of why the moves work. It also praises a joke that does not land, and the outline's claim that the close ends on recognition contradicts the rewrite's actual ending.

faults.quote: My mother went over right away, cookies in hand, because she wanted to know everything about them
faults.why: The outline says the close should end on the recognition. The rewrite instead tacks on an invented prediction, so the closing beat is weakened.

judge.verdict: The rewrite catches the mom/single-dad contradiction but mends it with an unsupported 'grandma', changes 'divorced' to 'separated', and ends on a garbled invented line. The Obama voice is thin, and the notes cite dubious sources and teach little.

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Hi team,

We're moving the launch from Tuesday to Thursday. Here's the thing: Legal hasn't signed off on the page with our prices yet, and that's why I don't want us shipping without it. Legal keeps its own clock.

Please have your parts of the deck done by the middle of the day on Wednesday. If you're blocked, don't wait — tell me today, not tomorrow.

plan.gist: Hi team
plan.why: He would open the same way: a short, direct address to the people he is asking to act, with no throat-clearing.

plan.gist: The launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
plan.why: He would state the decision first, plainly, so every reader knows at once what has changed and what the rest of the note hangs on.

plan.gist: Legal has not signed off on the pricing page, and we should not ship without it
plan.why: He would give the reason immediately after the decision, because the decision only persuades if the team sees it is not arbitrary but required.

plan.gist: Have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon
plan.why: He would turn the changed timeline into a concrete, dated ask, so the deadline is clear and each person knows their part.

plan.gist: If you are blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow
plan.why: He would close the ask by inviting early word of trouble, which protects the new date and turns the team from passive recipients into partners.

plan.gist: Thanks, Sam
plan.why: He would end with brief thanks, matching the warm but businesslike tone of the whole.

faults.quote: Legal keeps its own clock.
faults.why: This is an added sentence that does more than comment. It implies Legal is slow or on its own schedule, which the writer never said, and it softens the plain statement of the delay.

faults.quote: the page with our prices
faults.why: The writer's 'pricing page' is a term the team knows. Rewording it as 'the page with our prices' adds nothing and loosens the reference.

faults.quote: by the middle of the day on Wednesday
faults.why: This is a clumsy paraphrase of 'noon'. It makes the deadline vaguer, and the 'Wednesday at noon' deadline is a key fact.

faults.quote: don't wait —
faults.why: This adds an instruction to the writer's request. It is mild, but the writer only said to tell Sam today.

faults.quote: Here's the thing:
faults.why: This is a generic conversational filler in modern prose, not a distinctive Obama construction. It reads as costume and makes a flat decision sound like a confession.

faults.quote: and that's why I don't want us shipping without it
faults.why: The sentence is stiff and redundant. Obama would build a more rhythmic, principled line, such as a tricolon or a 'we owe it to...' appeal. The 'that's why' feels bolted on.

faults.quote: Thanks, Sam
faults.why: The sign-off is collapsed onto one line, which loses the email's closing form. The voice is barely changed from the original, so the rewrite is mostly a light paraphrase.

faults.quote: Legal keeps its own clock.
faults.why: This is an odd, slightly passive-aggressive idiom for a team email. It could read as a dig at Legal and sits awkwardly after the previous sentence.

faults.quote: cites President Barack Obama's State of the Union Address, 28 January 2014, ¶ 73
faults.why: The citations are precise-looking paragraph references for generic phrases like 'Here's the thing', and they are doubtful. They do not show a real, apt source for the move.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The voice's wry verdict on Legal's delay: a gentle, resigned observation that frames the hold-up without blaming anyone.
faults.why: The note claims the line avoids blame, but 'keeps its own clock' arguably does blame Legal. The note also admits the sentence is an addition, not a restyling.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:
  (no notes)
faults.why: The empty paragraph slots (1 and 4) make the notes look structurally mismatched, since the paragraph numbering does not match the email. The notes also leave the greeting and the sign-off unremarked.

faults.quote: closing each paragraph on where it lands rather than what happens next
faults.why: The advice is vague and does not match the rewrite, whose paragraphs do not end this way. The claim that the original 'rattles the news off' also overstates the difference.

faults.quote: The voice turns to the listener before the hard news
faults.why: The note claims the voice turns to the listener first, but the rewrite states the news first and only then says 'Here's the thing'. The note contradicts the text.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the email's form and facts mostly intact, but it is barely changed and adds a gratuitous remark about Legal. The voice is thin, the notes' claims partly contradict the text, and the lesson is vague.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

rewrite:
Here's the thing. Our town should shut Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare, and the walks are so narrow that a parent with a child can barely get through.

Towns across the country have already tried it, and their shops have never done better. Some shop owners will tell you their customers won't be able to reach them. The truth is, most folks are walking in from the lot anyway — and the customers they're worried about losing have been walking past their doors all along. They'll get used to it before long.

And that's why we should give it a try this summer.

faults.quote: a parent with a child can barely get through

faults.quote: the customers they're worried about losing have been walking past their doors all along

faults.quote: their shops have never done better

faults.quote: They'll get used to it before long.
faults.why: The 'they'll get used to it' point is now left dangling after the new irony. It is also unclear whether 'they' means owners or customers, so the dismissive tone is blurred.

faults.quote: Here's the thing.

faults.quote: most folks are walking in from the lot anyway

faults.quote: And that's why we should give it a try this summer.
faults.why: 'That's why' does not follow from what precedes it. The connective is a forced Obama tic, and the close is flat, with no appeal to community or shared purpose.

faults.quote: the walks are so narrow
faults.why: 'Walks' for sidewalks is slightly odd. The writer's sense is also weakened by 'so narrow that…' while the logic of the objection answer is muddled.

faults.quote: cites Weekly Address, 13 August 2011, ¶ 12

faults.quote: Begins your paragraph 1, which the next paragraph finishes.

faults.quote: Towns across the country have already tried it, and their shops have never done better. Some shop owners will tell you
faults.why: The evidence is placed before the objection, which is fine. But the objection and answer are fused with the added irony and lack a clear concession then rebuttal. The reasons paragraph is not given a proper build.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the skeleton but swaps the stroller for a vaguer image and adds an unsupported 'customers walking past their doors' claim. The Obama voice is thin, made of a few tics and flat sentences, and the notes' citations and the lesson are generic and partly inaccurate.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.

Here’s the thing: folks are burned out, and our best engineer just quit. So I believe we should move our workweek to four days.

The studies show that when people work fewer days, productivity doesn’t fall — it holds steady, and sometimes it rises. And it would make hiring easier besides.

Now, I know there’s risk in it, and some of our clients may not like it. But the truth is, if we wait until no one could object to anything, we’d never try anything at all. So let’s try it for three months, and then we’ll see where we stand.

lessons: Your draft opened with the policy and then listed reasons; Obama starts with the human cost, so the proposal arrives as a remedy, and closes each turn by looking at what it means for all of us and what we do next. It would help with hiring.
It is risky and clients might not like it.

plan.gist: People are burned out and our best engineer just quit.
plan.why: Begin with the human cost, not the policy, so the listener feels the urgency before being asked to decide anything.

plan.gist: Switch to a four-day week.
plan.why: After the cost is felt, the proposal arrives as a remedy to a named problem rather than an abstract preference.

plan.gist: Studies show productivity stays the same or goes up.
plan.why: Answer the listener's unspoken worry about harm with data, which buys confidence without overpromising.

plan.gist: It would also help with hiring.
plan.why: Extend the case from repairing burnout to building future strength, so the change serves the team's long-term interest.

plan.gist: It is risky and clients might not like it.
plan.why: Name the strongest counterargument aloud to show honesty and take the edge off the listener's doubt.

plan.gist: Try it for three months and see.
plan.why: Close with a limited, evidence-based trial: it answers the objection with prudence and turns the proposal into a small, reversible step rather than a leap.

faults.quote: The studies show that when people work fewer days, productivity doesn’t fall — it holds steady, and sometimes it rises.
faults.why: The writer said studies show productivity 'stays the same or goes up'. The rewrite adds a stated cause, 'when people work fewer days', and turns 'there are studies' into a definite 'The studies', which overstates the evidence slightly.

faults.quote: But the truth is, if we wait until no one could object to anything, we’d never try anything at all.
faults.why: This adds a new argument that the writer never made. It reads as a commentary flourish, but it shifts the answer to the objection from 'try it and see' to a claim about paralysis. That is an invention, and it makes the objection sound dismissed rather than acknowledged.

faults.quote: Now, I know there’s risk in it, and some of our clients may not like it.
faults.why: The writer's 'I know it's risky and clients might not like it' is kept. However, the 'hiring' reason is softened to 'easier besides', which tacks it on and loses its status as a separate reason.

faults.quote: Here’s the thing: folks are burned out
faults.why: 'Here's the thing' and 'folks' are surface Obama tics. The rest is plain modern workplace prose, with no Obama periodic build, parallel triads, or 'that's what…' turns. It reads as a costume.

faults.quote: So I believe we should move our workweek to four days.
faults.why: This is flat and generic. Obama would give the claim more rhythm or a moral frame, and the sentence does nothing distinctive.

faults.quote: cites Howard University Commencement Ceremony, 7 May 2016, ¶ 48
faults.why: The cited sources (Howard, Selma, Morehouse, Joplin, Weekly Address) are attached to ordinary sentences with no real parallel. The claimed paragraph numbers are unverifiable and the moves do not match the text.

faults.quote: Not this, but that: “The studies show that when people work fewer days, productivity doesn’t fall — it holds steady, and sometimes it rises.”
faults.why: This is not a real 'not this, but that' contrast. It is a plain restatement of the evidence, so the label is inaccurate.

faults.quote: Ironic verdict: “But the truth is, if we wait until no one could object...
faults.why: The line is not ironic. It is also a sentence the writer did not have, and the notes call it a 'liberty' without admitting it adds content.

faults.quote: Structure: Begins your paragraph 1, which the next paragraph finishes.
faults.why: The notes describe the splitting of the paragraph but do not explain why. The 'Liberty taken' items are vague, and 'Obama frames his own judgement modestly' does not describe a real change.

faults.quote: Here’s the thing: folks are burned out, and our best engineer just quit. So I believe we should move our workweek to four days.
faults.why: The outline claims the voice puts the problem first, but the writer's draft already led with the claim and the rewrite barely reorders anything. The 'how it is built' contrast overstates the change: the claim and reasons are close to the original order, so the lesson does not match what the rewrite did.

faults.quote: closes each turn by looking at what it means for all of us and what we do next.
faults.why: This is generic and not grounded in the text. The rewrite does not demonstrate it, and the lesson gives no concrete transferable technique beyond 'problem before claim'.

faults.quote: And it would make hiring easier besides.
faults.why: 'Besides' at the end of a clause is awkward and dated, and it is not an idiom Obama would use.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the facts and the order largely intact, but it invents an argument in the closing paragraph and the voice is mostly a few surface tics. The notes cite sources that do not match the sentences and mislabel the moves, and the lesson overstates how much was restructured.

When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.

When Dana told me she had to beg off our dinner, I didn't mind at all. The truth is, I was relieved. The whole week I'd been looking for a way out, and I won't pretend that sits well with me.

So I said it was no trouble, that we'd find another evening soon. But I don't believe we will, and that's the honest part.

notes.after: When Dana told me she had to beg off our dinner, I didn't mind at all. The truth is, I was relieved.

notes.cite: Armed Forces Farewell Ceremony for General Martin Dempsey, 25 September 2015, ¶ 5

lessons: The writer leans on flat little sentences. I gave each line a fuller clause and a turn at the end, so the relief and the unkept promise land with weight, and left the facts and feelings exactly as they were: relief, dread, the dinner that won't come.

outline.gist: Dana cancels the dinner she and the narrator had planned.
The narrator is not upset, but relieved.
The narrator had been dreading it all week and is not proud of that.
The narrator tells Dana it is fine and they will do it another time.
The narrator does not think they will.

plan.gist: Open on the concrete moment: Dana cancels the dinner.
plan.why: Beginning with the specific event puts the reader inside the scene before any feeling is explained, so the emotion that follows is anchored in something real.

plan.gist: State the surprising truth: I was not upset; I was relieved.
plan.why: Leading with the unexpected feeling earns attention and gives the reader the central emotional fact up front, rather than burying it.

plan.gist: Complicate the relief: I had been dreading it all week, and I am not proud of that.
plan.why: Adding the shame right after the relief keeps the narrator honest; the reader trusts a voice that names the mixed feeling instead of hiding it.

plan.gist: Give the outward words: I told her it was fine, we would do it another time.
plan.why: Showing what was actually said lets the reader measure the gap between the public response and the private feeling, which is where the story's meaning lives.

plan.gist: Close on the unspoken truth: I do not think we will.
plan.why: Ending on the quiet contradiction leaves the reader with the real point, the distance between what was promised and what the narrator believes, without over-explaining it.

faults.quote: The whole week I'd been looking for a way out
faults.why: The writer said she had been dreading the dinner. Looking for a way out is a different claim: it implies active scheming, and it changes the degree and nature of the feeling.

faults.quote: I won't pretend that sits well with me.
faults.why: The writer said 'I'm not proud of that.' Not sitting well is close but different, and the shame is softened into discomfort.

faults.quote: Dana told me she had to beg off
faults.why: Adds that Dana had to cancel, which implies necessity. The original only says she cancelled. It also changes 'cancelled' to a more colloquial idiom.

faults.quote: I said it was no trouble, that we'd find another evening soon.
faults.why: The writer said 'it was fine' and 'another time'. 'Soon' is added, and 'no trouble' shifts the meaning slightly.

faults.quote: and that's the honest part.
faults.why: This is a tacked-on commentary tag that sounds like a generic modern aside. It is not Obama's cadence, and it explains the turn the writer left unspoken.

faults.quote: I didn't mind at all.
faults.why: The register is flat and plain. There is almost no Obama signature: no balanced triads, no 'now' or 'look' pivot, no widening to a general reflection. The text is modern prose lightly costumed.

faults.quote: Not this, but that: “When Dana told me she had to beg off our dinner, I didn't mind at all. The truth is, I was relieved.” — cites A Memorial Service for the Victims of the Shooting in Tucson
faults.why: The quoted passage is not a not-this-but-that construction, and a Tucson memorial citation for a dinner cancellation is not apt. The citation looks fabricated.

faults.quote: Building in threes: “So I said it was no trouble, that we'd find another evening soon. But I don't believe we will, and that's the honest part.”
faults.why: There is no triad in the quoted lines. Two or three clauses are not a rule of three, so the note names a move that is not there.

faults.quote: From what happened to what we do: “But I don't believe we will, and that's the honest part.” — cites Weekly Address, 15 June 2013
faults.why: The line is a private admission, not a movement from event to action. The label is inaccurate.

faults.quote: The writer leans on flat little sentences. I gave each line a fuller clause and a turn at the end
faults.why: The lesson is generic and does not match the output, which is barely longer or fuller. It gives no concrete, reusable technique or reason.

faults.quote: As the voice would build it: event
faults.why: The outline of the voice's build merely restates the writer's order, with no Obama-specific structural move such as a pivot to a larger reflection. It adds little as a comparison.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the facts and the direction of feeling, but it blurs 'dreading' into 'looking for a way out', and the shame softens. The voice is thin and generic, the notes cite sources that do not show the moves named, and the lesson does not teach anything reusable.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan sent me word at midnight, and he said we needed to talk, and I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a place downtown where they sell coffee, and there he was when I got there, with his telephone in his hand and his thumb traveling over it, and he looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for anything serious, and he said it wasn't me but him—which is a thing people say when it is them.

I wanted to cry, but I didn't do it; I just nodded my head and said all right, and let it go at that. There was rain falling, and I walked home in it, and I ate a whole pint of ice cream when I got there.

My roommate reckoned I was carrying on over nothing, and maybe she was right, but it hurt all the same.

lessons: Your passage is told in short, separate sentences that state each fact alone; Twain's manner joins the facts into long "and… and…" runs that build to a turn, and lets the teller's voice carry the rueful joke—the punch line lands last, dry and unexplained. Practise stringing your clauses together and putting the one-liner at the end, without inventing any new event or feeling.

outline.gist: Midnight text from Ryan; narrator instantly reads it as a breakup.
Coffee shop meeting: Ryan already there, nervous, scrolling; he says he isn't ready for something serious and it isn't her, it's him.
Narrator doesn't cry, nods and says okay, walks home in the rain, eats a pint of ice cream.
Roommate says she is overreacting; narrator half-agrees but says it still hurt.

plan.gist: Open with the midnight text and the narrator's instant knowledge of what it meant.
plan.why: It starts in the middle of the event and gives the reader a question to carry into the next scene; the lesson is to open at the moment the trouble begins, not with the backstory before it.

plan.gist: Let the coffee shop do the telling: Ryan already there, nervous, phone in hand, then the two clichés he offers.
plan.why: The details answer the hook by showing the verdict arriving before it is spoken, so the reader feels it coming; the lesson is to let a scene deliver bad news through what the characters do and say, not by announcing it.

plan.gist: Show the hurt through what the narrator does: not crying, nodding, saying okay, walking in the rain, eating the whole pint.
plan.why: Restraint and small concrete actions make the feeling land harder than naming it; the lesson is to show feeling by behavior, then let the reader supply the emotion.

plan.gist: Close with the roommate's "overreacting" and the narrator's half-agreement, then the final line that it still hurt.
plan.why: The roommate voices the reader's possible judgment, and the last line answers it with the honest truth the whole piece was built to reach; the lesson is to end on the one sentence the story exists to say.

faults.quote: which is a thing people say when it is them
faults.why: Adds a new editorial claim and judgment. The writer's narrator did not mock Ryan's line, and this shifts the feeling toward sardonic distance. The notes call it a liberty, but it is more than commentary: it asserts that Ryan is lying.

faults.quote: and maybe she was right, but it hurt all the same
faults.why: The writer wrote 'Maybe I was' (overreacting), a self-doubt. The rewrite turns it into conceding the roommate's point, a shift in who holds the judgment. It also drops the quiet self-reproach.

faults.quote: carrying on over nothing
faults.why: The writer said 'overreacting'. 'Over nothing' is stronger and more dismissive, and it exaggerates the roommate's view.

faults.quote: a place downtown where they sell coffee
faults.why: Coy circumlocution for 'coffee shop' that reads as a riddle or parody rather than Twain's plain speech. A river-raised narrator would hardly be so coy about something ordinary.

faults.quote: with his telephone in his hand and his thumb traveling over it
faults.why: Stilted and anachronistic: 'telephone' and 'thumb traveling' read as a costume gag, and the word 'scrolling' is lost.

faults.quote: Ryan sent me word at midnight
faults.why: 'Sent me word' sounds like a messenger. It loses the texting medium in a muddle of period diction against modern content.

faults.quote: I wanted to cry, but I didn't do it; I just nodded my head and said all right, and let it go at that.
faults.why: 'Let it go at that' is added filler. The sentence is vernacular but flat, without Twain's comic specificity or understatement.

faults.quote: There was rain falling, and I walked home in it, and I ate a whole pint of ice cream when I got there.
faults.why: The ice cream gets no comic turn, and the sentence loses the effect of the writer's deadpan 'Then...'. It is a plain polysyndeton, not much of Twain's wit.

faults.quote: I ate a whole pint of ice cream when I got there
faults.why: Adds 'when I got there', a minor detail that the original did not give, since it only implies the eating happened at home.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 18, ¶ 83
faults.why: Precise chapter and paragraph citations are probably unverifiable or fabricated, and the cited passages are not shown to be apt for each move.

faults.quote: The voice sums up the numbness (nodded, said all right, did nothing more) in one quiet aside
faults.why: There is no aside in paragraph 3; the 'let it go at that' phrase is the only addition. The note describes something that is not there.

faults.quote: The narrator breaks off to give her dry verdict on the oldest speech in the world
faults.why: Claims the narrator is female and describes the aside as 'her' verdict, but the writer's gender is not given.

faults.quote: Practise stringing your clauses together and putting the one-liner at the end
faults.why: The advice is partly generic. The rewrite does not actually end on a one-liner punch: the last line is a flat 'it hurt all the same', so the lesson is not borne out by the text.

faults.quote: Ryan sent me word at midnight, and he said we needed to talk, and I knew right away what that meant.
faults.why: The structure is kept but the hook's compression is lost in the draggy 'and...and' chain; the one-beat 'I knew right away' lands less sharply.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the events and order but injects a sardonic claim about Ryan and softens the narrator's self-doubt, and several phrasings ('a place where they sell coffee', 'telephone... thumb traveling') read as parody rather than Twain. The notes also describe an aside that is not there and cite unverifiable passages.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

notes.text: An ironic verdict in the mother's own grasping way: she meant to set the daughter up with the new man, and he turns out divorced—wasted goods to a matchmaker; the joke is the voice's, adding no incident.
notes.after: it was a pity to have all that business wasted on a lawyer that was already used up

lessons: Your page is a plain list of short facts; Twain's is a man telling it, running clauses together with "and" and ending on a turn. Practise joining your sentences into one long run that builds to a joke, and let the narrator talk instead of report, and drop in one flat ironic verdict where the matter invites it.

outline.gist: A new family moves in next door last weekend; they have a huge truck and two little kids.
The dad seems nice; the mom is standoffish.
The narrator's mother bakes cookies and wants to learn everything: origin, work, church.
The dad is a lawyer and single—well, divorced.
The mother gets a look; the narrator knows exactly what she is thinking.
She has been trying to set the narrator up for years.

plan.gist: A new family moves in next door; huge truck, two little kids.
plan.why: Ground the anecdote in a plain, concrete neighborhood fact so the reader has a scene before the joke.

plan.gist: Dad seems nice; the woman with him is standoffish.
plan.why: Introduce the characters and the small friction, and let the reader see them as the narrator first sees them.

plan.gist: Mother bakes cookies and sets out to learn where they came from, what they do, whether they go to church.
plan.why: Show the mother's nosy, scheming nature, and make her investigation the engine that produces the key fact.

plan.gist: The dad is a lawyer and single—divorced.
plan.why: Deliver the turn only after the investigation, so the fact lands as news and changes the situation.

plan.gist: The mother gets a look; the narrator knows what it means.
plan.why: Let the reader share the narrator's recognition at the moment the scheme is born.

plan.gist: She has been trying to set the narrator up for years.
plan.why: End on the explanation as the punchline; it tells the reader why the look matters and that the narrator is in for it.

sense.problem: Your opening gives the new family a mother; three lines later the father is single—divorced. A household cannot have a wife and a single father at the same time.
sense.resolution: Keep the father single and divorced, because that fact is what sets up the mother's matchmaking and the whole joke. Change the standoffish woman so she is not his wife: 'His sister is kind of standoffish' (or 'the grandmother'). That removes the wife, keeps a female relative in the household, and leaves every other sentence true.
sense.quote: "The mom is kind of standoffish." ... "It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced."

faults.quote: his sister is kind of offish and unapproachable
faults.why: The writer's 'mom' is changed to the father's sister. The change mends the contradiction, but the sister is presented as a settled fact rather than a hedged guess, so it reads as an invented person. 'Unapproachable' also strengthens the writer's mild 'kind of standoffish'.

faults.quote: which I judge was owing to the truck and the moving, and not to any wish to be neighborly
faults.why: Adds a speculative explanation for the woman's standoffishness. The writer gave no cause, and this is invented content, not commentary. It also muddies the point, since it says she was not neighborly after all.

faults.quote: cakes
faults.why: The writer's cookies are changed to cakes, a small factual change with no reason given.

faults.quote: she would have had the whole of it out of them before they could set down a chair
faults.why: A hyperbolic addition that goes beyond the writer's 'wanted to find out everything'. The notes admit it is a liberty. It is a flourish, but it changes the mother's success from a wish to near-certain.

faults.quote: it was a pity to have all that business wasted on a lawyer that was already used up
faults.why: This inverts or garbles the writer's feeling. The writer's mother is hopeful and the narrator is wary. The rewrite makes the divorced lawyer 'used up' and the effort 'wasted', which contradicts the matchmaking look the passage just described. The 'business' is unclear: is it the cakes, or the years of trying to set the narrator up?

faults.quote: a lawyer that was already used up
faults.why: It is unclear and works as a riddle. Nothing in the passage supports calling him used up, and the line deflates the punchline instead of landing it.

faults.quote: they come with a great truck
faults.why: The dialect 'come' for 'came' is used inconsistently. 'It turned out' and 'was' appear alongside 'they come', so the voice wavers. Dialect verb forms such as 'the very day they come' are closer to Huck than to Twain's narrating voice in an anecdote like this.

faults.quote: My mother got that look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking—she has been trying to set me up for years
faults.why: This is mostly the writer's plain wording with the dash-joined run-on. The tense shift to 'has been' is not Twainian, and the ending lacks Twain's built-up cadence.

faults.quote: she has been trying to set me up for years, and it was a pity
faults.why: The writer's close (the years of trying) is buried and followed by a weaker, confusing extra clause. The punchline now ends on the lawyer rather than the narrator's fate.

faults.quote: Structure: Begins your paragraph 1, which the next paragraph finishes.
faults.why: This is a bare structural remark that teaches nothing. The notes cite specific chapters and paragraphs of Huckleberry Finn for moves ('Deadpan' at ch. 30, ¶ 45, for a plain sentence) whose aptness is doubtful.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: A small deadpan aside in the voice's idiom, adding nothing the passage did not imply.
faults.why: The note claims the aside adds nothing, but the cause of the woman's standoffishness is new content. The note also says the standoffish woman and the father's 'daughter' were set up, a 'daughter' that does not appear in the passage, so the notes misdescribe the rewrite.

faults.quote: changed the standoffish woman to his sister
faults.why: The mending is reported, and it fixes the contradiction. However, 'two little kids' now have no mother mentioned and the sister's presence is unexplained, so it is only a partial fix. It also makes it unclear whether the mother in the draft was the kids' mother.

judge.verdict: The rewrite catches and reports the single-father contradiction, but it adds invented explanation, swaps cookies for cakes, and ends on a muddled, mood-inverting joke ('already used up') that contradicts the mother's hopeful scheming. The dialect is uneven and the notes misdescribe parts of the rewrite.

lessons: Your memo was written in short, clipped office shorthand—a telegraph, not a letter. Launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
Legal has not signed off on the pricing page, and Sam will not ship without it
Deck sections due Wednesday at noon

plan.gist: Hi team
plan.why: A short greeting gives the email a human entry before business; it costs nothing and sets a cooperative tone.

plan.gist: Launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
plan.why: The changed date is the fact the team most needs first, because every following instruction depends on it.

plan.gist: Legal has not signed off on the pricing page, and Sam will not ship without it
plan.why: The reason follows immediately to answer the reader's natural 'why?' and to show the delay is principled, not casual.

plan.gist: Deck sections due Wednesday at noon
plan.why: The request comes after the announcement and reason so the reader sees the new deadline as the practical consequence of the new launch date.

plan.gist: If blocked, tell Sam today, not tomorrow
plan.why: The condition follows the request because it tells the reader exactly what to do if the deadline cannot be met, and 'today, not tomorrow' makes urgency concrete.

plan.gist: Thanks, Sam
plan.why: A brief close preserves goodwill and leaves the instruction standing without softening or repeating it.

faults.quote: and no use coming to me about it afterwards and saying you was blocked
faults.why: Adds a new admonition/scolding not in the original. Sam only asks to be told today if blocked. This changes the tone from helpful to reproachful.

faults.quote: the law has not made up its mind
faults.why: Recasts Legal (the internal legal team) as 'the law', an invented shift. The writer said Legal hasn't signed off, not that the law is undecided.

faults.quote: it ain’t no use shipping a page that the law ain’t approved of.
faults.why: Adds a redundant, new claim that restates and shifts the writer's reason ('I don't want us shipping without it') into a futility judgment; changes the stance from preference to uselessness.

faults.quote: I’ll give you the news in two lines
faults.why: Announced two lines but the message is not two lines; this is an invented framing. Also drops 'Quick update' sense awkwardly.

faults.quote: Legal ain’t signed off on the pricing page yet
faults.why: A single 'ain't' is costume; Twain's vernacular is Huck's, and applying it to a manager's office email reads as pastiche. There's no Twain-style narrator wit, digression, or extended comic simile; the voice is thin.

faults.quote: it ain’t no use shipping a page that the law ain’t approved of
faults.why: Stacked 'ain't' with a dangling 'of' and double negative reads clunky; the repeated 'ain't' and 'the law' repetition is garbled rather than deadpan.

faults.quote: you was blocked; if you’re blocked
faults.why: Switches from 'you was' dialect to standard 'you're' within one sentence; inconsistent register.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, “Chapter The Last”, ¶ 13
faults.why: Citations look fabricated or loosely apt; the same 'law has not made up its mind' is cited to two different works for two moves, and 'Cumulative sentence' is cited for a sentence that isn't cumulative.

faults.quote: The framing the voice lays over the writer's request, making the deadline a rule rather than just a plea; nothing new in the matter
faults.why: Claims nothing new was added, but the 'no use coming to me afterwards' scolding is new matter. Notes misreport the change; also no note on Paragraph 1 or 4 though greeting and sign-off were altered.

faults.quote: the law has not made up its mind
faults.why: Introduces a confusion about who is deciding (the law vs. the company's Legal team), a fault of sense in a text that had none.

faults.quote: running the clauses together on and and so the whole thing rides to the deadline at the end
faults.why: The lesson advocates and-chaining, yet the rewrite doesn't do it and the deadline is not the last line; the advice doesn't match the output and the structure outline is generic and says the voice builds it identically.

faults.quote: Thanks, Sam.
faults.why: The sign-off is collapsed into one line, losing the letter's closing form; the greeting is also altered to 'Hi, team.'

judge.verdict: The rewrite sprinkles 'ain't' over an office email, adds a scolding clause and a shaky 'the law' joke that alter Sam's helpful tone and meaning, and its notes misreport these changes. The lesson and structure analysis are generic and don't match what was written.

Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
We had ought to close up Main Street against the cars of a Saturday and a Sunday, and leave the whole of it to the town. For a man that wants to put his wagon somewheres downtown, there ain't any place to put it, and the sidewalks is that narrow a lady can't hardly push a carriage along without running somebody down; and it's a bad business from the first, and worse the longer you look at it. Other towns has tried it, and their shops is doing better than ever they done before, and no two ways about it.

I know there is some that keeps store in the place that will set up a holler, and say the customers can't get to them no more. But the owners will get used to it, I judge. The truth of it is, most folks already walks up from where they leave the wagon, anyway.

We had ought to try it this summer. The long and the short of it is, Main Street could use a rest, and the cars could use the exercise.

notes.text: Your second paragraph has two possible plural antecedents, 'business owners' and 'customers'; in 'But they'll get used to it,' the reader cannot tell who will get used to the closing. The next sentence answers the customers' side by saying most people walk anyway, so the 'they' should be the owners. I wrote 'the owners' instead of 'they', the least change, and it agrees with the following sentence.

notes.text: The voice closes with an ironic verdict on the writer's own proposal, in Twain's manner: putting the matter so that the street and the cars trade their usual parts. It frames what is there rather than adding an incident.

lessons: Your draft is stated like a town council resolution; Twain would hand the whole matter to a plain-spoken citizen grousing on a corner. The chief change is the voice: let a narrator talk it through in his own grammar, build the argument to its point, then land it flat and let it sit.

outline.gist: Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends.
Parking downtown is a nightmare; sidewalks too narrow for strollers.
Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.
Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them.
They'll get used to it; most people walk from the garage anyway.
We should try it this summer.

plan.gist: Open with the proposition: close Main Street to cars on weekends.
plan.why: It gives the reader one clear ask up front, so every later reason and answer is measured against it instead of leaving the reader to guess what is being urged.

plan.gist: Name the two felt nuisances: parking is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers.
plan.why: It grounds the claim in daily annoyances the reader has likely experienced, so the proposal reads as a remedy rather than a rule.

plan.gist: Bring in the other towns whose shops are doing better after doing the same.
plan.why: It anticipates the unspoken fear—will this hurt business?—and answers it with an outside example before the objection is named, so the objection arrives already weakened.

plan.gist: State the business owners' complaint fairly: customers can't get to them.
plan.why: Naming the strongest resistance makes the argument trustworthy; the reader believes a writer who admits the other side rather than hiding it.

plan.gist: Answer it: the owners will get used to it, and most people walk from the garage anyway.
plan.why: It disposes of the objection with the writer's best fact—people already arrive on foot—so closing the street changes less than the owners fear.

plan.gist: Close with the small experiment: try it this summer.
plan.why: It turns agreement into a limited, low-risk action, leaving the reader with something to do rather than only a position to hold.

sense.problem: The second paragraph has two possible plural antecedents, 'business owners' and 'customers'; in 'But they'll get used to it,' the reader cannot tell who will get used to the closing.
sense.resolution: Write 'But the owners will get used to it' (or 'business owners'). That is the least change, and it agrees with the next sentence, which already answers the customers' side by saying most people walk from the garage anyway.
sense.quote: Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it.

faults.quote: For a man that wants to put his wagon somewheres downtown, there ain't any place to put it
faults.why: The draft says parking is a nightmare. 'No place to put it' is a harsher claim, and the shift from cars to wagons changes the facts as well as the idiom.

faults.quote: and it's a bad business from the first, and worse the longer you look at it.
faults.why: This is invented commentary that goes beyond the writer's claim. It heightens the complaint and adds a new evaluative claim.

faults.quote: a lady can't hardly push a carriage along without running somebody down
faults.why: The draft says the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. The rewrite adds a result, collisions with pedestrians, which the writer never claimed. It also swaps 'strollers' for 'carriage' and 'lady'.

faults.quote: the cars of a Saturday and a Sunday
faults.why: The draft says 'weekends'. The rewrite is acceptable here, but 'against the cars' beside 'wagon' is inconsistent: the town has cars in one sentence and wagons in the next.

faults.quote: most folks already walks up from where they leave the wagon
faults.why: The draft refers to a garage. The rewrite changes it to 'where they leave the wagon', which is anachronistic and loses the garage. The 'folks … walks' agreement is also inconsistent with 'folks … that keeps' and 'they leave'.

faults.quote: the cars could use the exercise
faults.why: The closing joke is modern and cute. It reads as a punchline in costume rather than Twain's deadpan, and it is jarring to find cars here after the wagon talk.

faults.quote: Polysyndeton: “The truth of it is, most folks already walks up from where they leave the wagon, anyway.”
faults.why: The sentence contains no polysyndeton, so the label is wrong. The cited sources look unverifiable or misattributed, for example Tom Sawyer ch. 31, which does not fit 'We had ought to', and Innocents Abroad ch. 27 for deadpan.

faults.quote: Cumulative sentence: “For a man that wants to put his wagon somewheres downtown…
faults.why: The note names a move but does not mention that the rewrite adds 'bad business… worse the longer you look', an addition to the claim that should be disclosed as a liberty.

faults.quote: But the owners will get used to it, I judge.
faults.why: The mending is reported, but the draft's weak answer is only patched. 'Used to it' sits awkwardly against the customers' complaint, and the answer is not strengthened or restructured.

faults.quote: The truth of it is, most folks already walks up
faults.why: The order is kept, but the rewrite does not follow the notes' claim of building the argument differently. The lesson says 'build the argument to its point', yet nothing was restructured.

faults.quote: Your draft is stated like a town council resolution; Twain would hand the whole matter to a plain-spoken citizen grousing on a corner.
faults.why: The lesson is generic and mostly about voice. It gives no concrete reusable technique, such as how a narrator's aside lets an argument concede a point, or why the flat landing works.

faults.quote: We had ought to close up Main Street
faults.why: Dialect is applied generically, with 'ain't', 'is that narrow' and 'has tried', in a Huck-like register. Twain's own essayistic voice has more irony and longer periodic build. The result is caricature rather than Twain's argumentative wit.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the argument's skeleton and has some Twain-flavored dialect, but it adds claims (collisions, 'bad business'), muddles wagons and cars, and ends on a cute modern joke. The notes mislabel moves and the lesson is thin.

I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
The hands are wore out, and the best engineer we had has up and quit, and I judge it don't pay a man to wear himself down to a rag for four days' wages, nor for five. So I judge it might could be helped if we cut the week down to four days and done with it. There's studies that show the work stays the same or gets better for it, and it would be a help in hiring, too.

I know it's risky, and the clients may not like it, and I don't say they will; but we could try it for three months and see how she goes.

rows.text: The hands are wore out, and the best engineer we had has up and quit, and I judge it don't pay a man to wear himself down to a rag for four days' wages, nor for five. So I judge it might could be helped if we cut the week down to four days and done with it. There's studies that show the work stays the same or gets better for it, and it would be a help in hiring, too.

notes.after: The hands are wore out, and the best engineer we had has up and quit.
and done with it.
I judge it might could be helped if we cut the week down to four days.
it don't pay a man to wear himself down to a rag for four days' wages, nor for five.

notes.text: The voice pauses to judge the matter in its own words — a flat generalization the situation invites — which turns the staff's being burned out from a fact into a verdict the reader already half agrees with, and lets the proposal arrive as the remedy.
notes.after: it don't pay a man to wear himself down to a rag for four days' wages, nor for five.

rows.text: I know it's risky, and the clients may not like it, and I don't say they will; but we could try it for three months and see how she goes.

notes.after: the clients may not like it, and I don't say they will.
notes.cite: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court, ch. 33, ¶ 1

notes.after: we could try it for three months and see how she goes.

lessons: The writer flung the proposal out first and let each bit of proof stand apart as a bare claim. Twain would begin with the human fact — the hands wore out and the best engineer gone — so the reader feels the need before the remedy is named, then let the rest run on in one long easy sentence until the trial closes it. The voice talks like Huck, plain and worn in the grammar, and rests its case in a dry verdict rather than in an argument.

outline.gist: Switch to a four-day week.
People are burned out; best engineer just quit.
Studies show productivity stays the same or goes up.
It would help with hiring.
It is risky; clients might not like it.
Try it for three months and see.

plan.gist: Begin with the human fact: the staff are burned out and the best engineer just quit.
plan.why: A concrete, felt event makes the reader want a remedy before the remedy is named; it is stronger than starting with the abstract proposal.

plan.gist: Then propose the four-day week.
plan.why: Once the reader feels the problem, the proposal lands as an answer, not as an unsupported opinion.

plan.gist: Bring in the studies that productivity stays the same or rises.
plan.why: It answers the reader's first worry—will less time mean less work?—with outside proof.

plan.gist: Add that it would help hiring.
plan.why: A practical advantage widens the appeal beyond the present staff to the company's future.

plan.gist: Concede the risk and that clients may dislike it.
plan.why: Naming the downside yourself builds trust and shows the proposal has been thought through, not wished for.

plan.gist: Close with the three-month trial.
plan.why: A small, reversible test lowers the cost of saying yes and turns the objection into a checkable experiment.

faults.quote: I judge it don't pay a man to wear himself down to a rag for four days' wages, nor for five.
faults.why: This adds a new claim about wages and pay (four days' wages versus five) that the writer never made. It is not commentary on what is there; it brings in a pay issue and muddles the burnout point.

faults.quote: The hands are wore out
faults.why: The writer said 'People are burned out'. 'Hands' recasts them as laborers and loses the writer's meaning, and 'wore out' is physical tiredness, not burnout.

faults.quote: and I don't say they will
faults.why: This softens the writer's 'clients might not like it' and adds a hedge the writer did not make. It changes the degree of the concern.

faults.quote: it might could be helped if we cut the week down to four days and done with it
faults.why: The writer's firm 'we should switch' becomes a tentative 'might could be helped'. 'And done with it' adds a note of finality the writer did not intend, so the force of the proposal changes.

faults.quote: So I judge it might could be helped
faults.why: The 'So' follows the wages remark, and 'it' has no clear referent. The causal chain from burnout to the proposal is muddy.

faults.quote: I judge it don't pay a man
faults.why: The voice is mostly Huck dialect, and the sentence is a flat moral. Twain's irony and exaggeration, his comic similes, and the deadpan build-up and reversal are mostly absent. It reads as generic rural dialect, not Twain's narrative wit.

faults.quote: might could be helped
faults.why: The double modal is Southern dialect, but 'it might could be helped' is an awkward construction for the proposal and is not Twain's idiom.

faults.quote: for four days' wages, nor for five
faults.why: The phrase is unclear. Read as a riddle, it suggests the staff are underpaid, which has nothing to do with the original.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 32, ¶ 51
faults.why: 'and done with it' is called a 'narrator's aside', but it is a plain phrase. The citations look invented and do not plainly match the quoted lines. The Pudd'nhead Wilson and Connecticut Yankee citations are also doubtful.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The voice pauses to judge the matter in its own words
faults.why: This admits adding a verdict but does not flag that it brings in a wages claim. It presents invented content as harmless commentary.

faults.quote: Cumulative sentence: “I judge it might could be helped if we cut the week down to four days.”
faults.why: The sentence is short and not cumulative, so the label is inaccurate.

faults.quote: The hands are wore out, and the best engineer we had has up and quit
faults.why: The how_it_is_built and the lesson promise one long, easy sentence, and the rewrite puts evidence first. But the studies and hiring points are still two short clauses, and the proposal comes after a muddled verdict. The reordering is only partly carried out.

faults.quote: rests its case in a dry verdict rather than in an argument
faults.why: The lesson is vague and partly contradicted by the rewrite, since the verdict contains an invented claim. It does not give concrete, reusable moves such as understatement, the concrete comparison, or the deadpan reversal.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is in Huck-style dialect, not Twain's wit, and it adds a wages claim the writer never made. It also weakens the proposal's firmness and leaves the opening muddled. The notes cite doubtful sources and the lesson is thin.

yours:
When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana cancelled our dinner, not a mite upset, I warn't. I was relieved, and I don't mind owning it. I'd been dreading it all the week through, and I ain't proud of it, neither.

I told her it was all right, and another time would do as well. I don't hardly think we will.

lessons: The writer's page is short, flat, and modern, with contractions running heavy and no narrator's voice in it. Twain lets a man tell it aloud the way he would, drawing the sentence out into a long run of ands, and he leaves the joke short at the end for it to land. Practise reading each sentence over as speech and letting the voice carry the feeling instead of naming it.

outline.gist: Dana cancelled the dinner.
The narrator was not upset but relieved.
The narrator had been dreading it all week and is not proud of that.
The narrator told Dana it was fine and they would do it another time.
The narrator does not think they will.

plan.gist: Dana cancelled; the narrator was not upset but relieved.
plan.why: It hooks the reader with a confession that reverses the expected social feeling, and puts the whole matter before us at once.

plan.gist: The narrator had been dreading it all week and is not proud of that.
plan.why: It explains the relief and shows the narrator is honest enough about a shameful feeling for the reader to trust the telling.

plan.gist: The narrator told Dana it was fine and they would do it another time.
plan.why: It gives the polite social surface set against the private truth, so the gap between them becomes the point.

plan.gist: The narrator does not think they will.
plan.why: It lands the meaning in a quiet verdict: the dinner, and likely the friendship, is over; the small lie is left to sit with the reader.

faults.quote: and I don't mind owning it
faults.why: Added clause. The writer says only that they are relieved and not proud of it. 'Don't mind owning it' is a new attitude (unashamed candor), and it sits uneasily beside 'I ain't proud of it' in the next sentence.

faults.quote: not a mite upset, I warn't
faults.why: Huck's dialect is pushed hard and the inverted tag is closer to Yankee/Irish idiom than Twain's. The register is also inconsistent: 'I warn't' and 'ain't' sit beside the polished 'owning it' and 'would do as well', so it reads as dialect in costume.

faults.quote: I don't hardly think we will.
faults.why: 'Don't hardly' is a double negative that says 'I scarcely think' and weakens the writer's flat 'I don't think we will'. The doubt becomes milder, and 'we will' has nothing to attach to once 'do it another time' became 'another time would do as well'.

faults.quote: all the week through
faults.why: An awkward, unidiomatic phrase. Twain would say 'all the week' or 'the whole week'.

faults.quote: I told her it was all right, and another time would do as well.
faults.why: 'Would do as well' is stiff and genteel, not a Huck-like or Twain-like phrase. The writer's 'we'd do it another time' also becomes a general remark, which loses 'we'.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 17, ¶ 54
faults.why: The citations are precise-looking but not verifiable and apparently invented. The quoted lines are the rewriter's own, not passages from these chapters, and the 'cumulative sentence' cited to ch. 3 is not a cumulative run of ands.

faults.quote: [liberty] Liberty taken: The writer confesses the dreading without judging it; the voice adds the plain self-judgment
faults.why: The writer already says 'I'm not proud of that', so the claim that the rewrite adds self-judgment is wrong. The notes also fail to flag the added 'I don't mind owning it' as a real change.

faults.quote: drawing the sentence out into a long run of ands
faults.why: The lesson says Twain draws sentences into a run of ands and leaves the joke short, but the rewrite does neither. It has no long run of ands and keeps the choppy sentences, so the lesson does not match the output, and the notes give the writer little to reuse.

faults.quote: I was relieved, and I don't mind owning it. I'd been dreading it
faults.why: The outline calls for a hook that reverses the social expectation, but the rewrite buries the reversal in a dialect inversion. The close is also weakened by 'hardly', and the reason is not compressed or sharpened.

judge.verdict: Faithful in feeling and clear, but the voice is surface dialect with a stray added attitude ('don't mind owning it') and a softened ending ('don't hardly'). The notes' citations look invented and mislabel the changes, and the lesson describes moves the rewrite does not make.
